Knowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching:
Frozen Estimation and Adaptation

Yian HuangKnowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching:
Frozen Estimation and Adaptation    Jian HuangKnowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching:
Frozen Estimation and AdaptationThe Hong Kong Polytechnic University    yian.huang@polyu.edu.hk   j.huang@polyu.edu.hk
Abstract

Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.

1 Introduction

Conditional generative modeling seeks to recover the distribution of a response given its covariates (Zhou et al., 2023). A distributional description accommodates heterogeneity, tail behavior, and dependence, and supports prediction beyond the conditional mean (Meinshausen, 2006; Ćevid et al., 2022). In applications with limited observations from the population of interest, a related source population can provide valuable information about how the covariates should be represented (Maurer et al., 2016; Tripuraneni et al., 2020). This opportunity is especially attractive when a high-dimensional context acts through a lower-dimensional feature map (Lee et al., 2013). Transferring that map can concentrate target learning on the task-specific distribution, while allowing the source and target response laws, and even their response dimensions, to differ (Tian and Shen, 2026).

Continuous normalizing flows construct distributions by transporting a reference law through an ordinary differential equation (Chen et al., 2018). Flow matching learns the transporting velocity through regression against velocities associated with a prescribed probability path (Lipman et al., 2023). This formulation provides a direct route to representation transfer for conditional generation: a source encoder summarizes common covariates, and a target velocity head combines this summary with the current state, time, and any task-specific covariates. With independent source and target samples of sizes nsn_{s} and ntn_{t}, the statistical objective is to use the information in the source sample to improve the conditional distribution generated for the target task.

Two complementary uses of a source representation are particularly useful. Freezing the representation reduces target fitting to learning a velocity head with a smaller input dimension. Adapting it permits the target sample to recover additional relevant information. The structure of the required change is central: a smooth correction involving a few context coordinates can be considerably easier to estimate than a new representation of the entire context. This observation motivates an analysis that distinguishes the information supplied by the source, the complexity of a target correction, and the accuracy of the resulting generated distribution.

We develop this analysis for two procedures, TFM-Freeze and TFM-Adapt. TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head while retaining the source-fitted encoder. TFM-Adapt jointly estimates a target head and an updated representation, with a functional penalty that anchors the representation to its source fit. An independent validation step then compares the generated conditional distributions and permits a data-dependent choice between transfer and target-only learning.

1.1 Main contributions

The paper makes four principal contributions.

  1. 1.

    Statistical guarantees from source learning to generation. We establish explicit neural risk bounds for frozen transfer and a target-only counterpart under stated smoothness and flow regularity conditions, with source-to-target calibration for frozen transfer (Theorems 1 and 3). The bounds account for joint estimation of the source encoder and head, target fitting, representation discrepancy, and numerical integration. They identify how a sufficiently informative source sample can reduce the representation-learning contribution to target risk. The analysis uses constructive ReLU approximations that simultaneously control function values and the actual state, representation, and time Lipschitz constants needed for generation.

  2. 2.

    A quantitative benefit from learning target corrections. Under smooth correctability, we compare TFM-Adapt and TFM-Freeze using the same source fit and the same target head class (Theorem 2). Adaptation replaces a frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the adaptation. The target complexity counts the fitted head and adaptation. The resulting comparison identifies regimes in which learning a correction improves the corresponding risk bound over freezing and reduces the representation-learning contribution relative to fitting the full target representation from scratch.

  3. 3.

    A strict advantage in actual generation risk. We derive an information lower bound for every generator whose evaluation-time context is restricted to the frozen representation together with the task-specific covariates. The bound is determined by the component of the target conditional mean that this reduced context does not retain. When this information loss dominates the remaining estimation and integration errors and the anchoring weight tends to zero, the adaptive generator achieves a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator using only the frozen context information (Corollaries 3.1 and C.6). A fully specified conditional-flow example verifies the conditions and exhibits both vanishing adaptive risk under fixed mismatch and a polynomial-rate separation under shrinking mismatch (Proposition D.1).

  4. 4.

    Validation with protection for negative transfer. We construct an independent energy-score validation rule for a finite dictionary of deployed conditional generators, including a target-only candidate. Under bounded endpoint support, selection satisfies a leading-constant-one oracle inequality in conditional energy risk. A conservative switching rule also guarantees, with the prescribed high probability, no deterioration relative to the fitted target-only generator (Theorem 4). Validation only requires one observed response at each sampled context and simulated draws from each candidate. The procedure thus provides a direct distributional criterion for deciding when to retain transfer.

Simulation studies with nonlinear representations, heteroscedasticity, and mixture responses illustrate the gains available from adaptation. Applications to superconducting materials and diamond prices further demonstrate the value of combining transfer with target validation.

1.2 Related literature

Our work connects four strands of literature.

Statistical transfer and shared representations.

Statistical transfer theory quantifies how the relation between source and target populations determines the value of auxiliary observations. Cai and Wei (2021) characterize this relation through minimax rates for nonparametric classification. For high-dimensional linear regression, Li et al. (2022) establish gains from informative auxiliary studies and use aggregation to obtain an oracle comparison that includes a target-only estimator. In shared representation learning, Tripuraneni et al. (2020) separate the complexity of estimating a common representation from that of learning a new task and quantify the role of task diversity. For generative models, Tian and Shen (2026) introduce a shared-embedding framework and establish distributional error bounds for diffusion models and coupling flows. The present paper studies conditional flow matching and also considers learning target adaptation, with explicit adaptation complexity and a frozen-information lower bound.

Flow matching and distributional error analysis.

The regression formulation of Lipman et al. (2023) gives a tractable conditional objective with the same population gradient as the marginal flow-matching loss. Benton et al. (2024) bound Wasserstein error by integrated velocity approximation error under spatial Lipschitz control. Gao et al. (2024) develop Gaussian interpolation flows and establish well-posedness, Lipschitz regularity, and Wasserstein stability under perturbations of the velocity field. More recent statistical analyses establish nearly minimax Wasserstein convergence rates over smooth density classes with suitable probability paths (Fukumizu et al., 2025) and account for neural estimation and Euler discretization in convergence guarantees for deep flow-matching estimators (Zhou and Liu, 2025). These results provide a foundation for studying the accuracy of a fitted flow. Our analysis addresses the additional statistical structure created by an estimated source representation and a target correction, and links that structure to both upper bounds and an information-based separation between adaptive and frozen generation.

Neural approximation and statistical estimation.

Quantitative approximation theory for ReLU networks includes uniform approximation over smooth function classes (Yarotsky, 2017) and Sobolev approximation that controls function values together with first weak derivatives (Gühring et al., 2020). Schmidt-Hieber (2020) derives statistical risk bounds for sparse ReLU regression estimators under compositional structure, with rates that reflect the dimensions of the component functions. These developments motivate explicit treatment of both approximation accuracy and the complexity of the functions estimated from data. For transferred conditional flows, we construct admissible approximants under prescribed blockwise Lipschitz budgets and account separately for source learning, the target head, and the adaptation.

Proper scoring rules and distributional validation.

Gneiting and Raftery (2007) develop strictly proper scoring rules for probabilistic prediction, including the energy score and its CRPS specialization. Sejdinovic et al. (2013) establish the equivalence between energy distance and squared distances between kernel mean embeddings for the corresponding kernels. These results provide the distributional and Hilbert-space foundations for energy-score assessment. We use this foundation to validate conditional endpoint laws with continuously distributed contexts, explicitly account for score simulation, and derive a finite-dictionary oracle inequality together with a confidence-calibrated switch from target-only generation to transfer.

Section 2 introduces the sampling framework, neural classes, and training procedures. Section 3 presents the transfer bounds, adaptation comparison, information lower bound, and target-only counterpart. Section 4 develops endpoint validation. Sections 5 and 6 report the simulation studies and real-data applications. The appendices contain the proofs, constructive approximation results, and numerical details.

The constants bj,Lx,j,Lu,j,Lτ,jb_{j},L_{x,j},L_{u,j},L_{\tau,j} are fixed and positive. Each blockwise Lipschitz constant varies only its indicated argument, with all other arguments held fixed. Set BV,j=dj​bjB_{V,j}=\sqrt{d_{j}}\,b_{j}. These heads are globally defined, bounded by BV,jB_{V,j}, and satisfy Equation 2.15 outside the training rectangle as well. Lemma B.2 constructs approximants satisfying the actual constraints, and Proposition B.3 gives a finite cell-slope characterization.

2.4 The two training algorithms

We introduce our proposed algorithms in the following. A measurable ϵ\epsilon-minimizer of an objective JJ over a nonempty class means an output θ^\widehat{\theta} satisfying J⁡(θ^)≤infθJ⁡(θ)+ϵJ(\widehat{\theta})\leq\inf_{\theta}J(\theta)+\epsilon. We use tolerances ns−2n_{s}^{-2} and nt−2n_{t}^{-2}. This defines the statistical estimators without asserting a convergence guarantee for a particular numerical optimizer. The resolution parameters Ns,Ms,NtN_{s},M_{s},N_{t} are fixed before training; their rate-optimal choices are given in Equation 3.6.

 

Algorithm 1 (TFM-Freeze).

Input: independent source and target training samples; head sieves 𝒱s,Ns,𝒱t,Nt\mathcal{V}_{s,N_{s}},\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}}; representation sieve ℋMs\mathcal{H}_{M_{s}}.

  1. 1.

    On the source sample, compute

    ℒ^s​(v^s,h^s)≤infv∈𝒱s,Ns,h∈ℋMsℒ^s​(v,h)+ns−2.\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{s}(\widehat{v}_{s},\widehat{h}_{s})\leq\inf_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{s,N_{s}},\,h\in\mathcal{H}_{M_{s}}}\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{s}(v,h)+n_{s}^{-2}. (2.16)
  2. 2.

    Keep h^s\widehat{h}_{s} fixed. On the target sample, compute

    ℒ^t​(v^F,h^s)≤infv∈𝒱t,Ntℒ^t​(v,h^s)+nt−2.\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{t}(\widehat{v}_{F},\widehat{h}_{s})\leq\inf_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}}}\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{t}(v,\widehat{h}_{s})+n_{t}^{-2}. (2.17)
  3. 3.

    Return F^F=Ft,v^F,h^s\widehat{F}_{F}=F_{t,\widehat{v}_{F},\widehat{h}_{s}}. Generate using Equation 2.7, exactly or by JJ Euler steps.

 

For functional anchoring, let 𝒟a={za,i:1≤i≤na}\mathscr{D}_{a}=\{z_{a,i}:1\leq i\leq n_{a}\} be a declared design of common-block contexts, independent of the target training sample and its auxiliary draws. The design may be deterministic or source-derived. A default empirical functional anchor is

As​(h)=1na​∑i=1na‖h⁡(za,i)−h^s​(za,i)‖2.A_{s}(h)=\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{a}}\|h(z_{a,i})-\widehat{h}_{s}(z_{a,i})\|^{2}. (2.18)

A second, mathematically defined functional anchor is

As∞​(h)=supz0∈𝒵0‖h⁡(z0)−h^s​(z0)‖2.A_{s}^{\infty}(h)=\sup_{z_{0}\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}}\|h(z_{0})-\widehat{h}_{s}(z_{0})\|^{2}. (2.19)

Either is a discrepancy between representation functions, not a distance between network weight vectors. In particular, reparameterizations of network weights that preserve the function do not change the anchor. Other nonnegative functional anchors with As​(h^s)=0A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s})=0 are allowed when the conditions of the particular theorem being used are verified.

 

Algorithm 2 (TFM-Adapt with a functional anchor).

Input: independent source and target training samples; a target-independent anchor design; a fixed λ≥0\lambda\geq 0.

  1. 1.

    Compute (v^s,h^s)(\widehat{v}_{s},\widehat{h}_{s}) by Equation 2.16. Construct the functional anchor AsA_{s}, for example Equation 2.18.

  2. 2.

    Choose a declared bounded-output neural encoder class ℋA\mathcal{H}_{A} containing the source fit h^s\widehat{h}_{s}. The class may depend on source training and the anchor design, but not on target training. Jointly fit (v^λ,h^λ)∈𝒱t,Nt×ℋA(\widehat{v}_{\lambda},\widehat{h}_{\lambda})\in\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}}\times\mathcal{H}_{A} so that

    ℒ^t​(v^λ,h^λ)+λ​As​(h^λ)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{t}(\widehat{v}_{\lambda},\widehat{h}_{\lambda})+\lambda A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda}) ≤infv∈𝒱t,Nt,h∈ℋA{ℒ^t​(v,h)+λ​As​(h)}+nt−2.\displaystyle\leq\inf_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}},\,h\in\mathcal{H}_{A}}\{\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{t}(v,h)+\lambda A_{s}(h)\}+n_{t}^{-2}. (2.20)
  3. 3.

    Return F^λ=Ft,v^λ,h^λ\widehat{F}_{\lambda}=F_{t,\widehat{v}_{\lambda},\widehat{h}_{\lambda}}. Generate using Equation 2.7, exactly or by JJ Euler steps.

 

At λ=0\lambda=0, Equation 2.20 defines unpenalized joint fitting over the same declared class 𝒱t,Nt×ℋA\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}}\times\mathcal{H}_{A}.

3 Theoretical guarantees

3.1 Assumptions and explicit rates

Assumption 1 (Regression experiment and true flow).

For j=s,tj=s,t, there is a fixed BU,j<∞B_{U,j}<\infty such that ‖Uj,T‖≤BU,j\|U_{j,T}\|\leq B_{U,j} almost surely, and Sj,T∈[−Kx,j,Kx,j]djS_{j,T}\in[-K_{x,j},K_{x,j}]^{d_{j}} almost surely. For almost every context zz, the true velocity vj0v_{j}^{0} has a unique characteristic solution Φj,τ​(g,z)\Phi_{j,\tau}(g,z) on [0,1][0,1], for γj\gamma_{j}-almost every initial gg, whose law at time τ\tau is ℒ⁡(Sj,τ∣Zj=z)\mathcal{L}(S_{j,\tau}\mid Z_{j}=z). These characteristics have integrable second moments. All conditional versions used in the ODE are jointly measurable.

For a>0a>0, write k=⌈a⌉−1k=\lceil a\rceil-1 and α=a−k∈(0,1]\alpha=a-k\in(0,1]. The class Ca​(K,B)C^{a}(K;B) consists of functions on a fixed rectangle KK with derivatives through order kk bounded by BB, and derivatives of order kk that are α\alpha-Hölder with constant BB. We use Euclidean output norms and Euclidean input distance. At integer aa, this means Lipschitz derivatives of order a−1a-1. Derivatives are continuous up to the boundary.

Assumption 2 (Smooth task-specific comparison functions).

For each task to which this assumption is applied, fix rj>1r_{j}>1, βj>0\beta_{j}>0, and finite positive smoothness bounds. There are functions hj,0∈Cβj​(𝒵0,Bh,j)h_{j,0}\in C^{\beta_{j}}(\mathcal{Z}_{0};B_{h,j}), taking values in [−1,1]dh[-1,1]^{d_{h}}, and gj,0∈Crj​(𝒦j,Bg,j)g_{j,0}\in C^{r_{j}}(\mathcal{K}_{j};B_{g,j}), taking values in [−bj,bj]dj[-b_{j},b_{j}]^{d_{j}}, such that

ζj2:=‖vj0−gj,0​(⋅,hj,0​(⋅),⋅,⋅)‖j2<∞.\zeta_{j}^{2}:=\|v_{j}^{0}-g_{j,0}(\,\cdot,h_{j,0}(\,\cdot),\,\cdot,\,\cdot)\|_{j}^{2}<\infty. (3.1)

For positive fixed margins ηx,j,ηu,j,ητ,j\eta_{x,j},\eta_{u,j},\eta_{\tau,j},

Lipb⁡(gj,0;𝒦j)≤Lb,j−ηb,j,b∈{x,u,τ}.\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(g_{j,0};\mathcal{K}_{j})\leq L_{b,j}-\eta_{b,j},\qquad b\in\{x,u,\tau\}. (3.2)

The source and target comparison representations need not be identical. Exact shared structure is the special case hs,0=ht,0=h0h_{s,0}=h_{t,0}=h_{0} and ζs=ζt=0\zeta_{s}=\zeta_{t}=0.

The notation in Equation 3.1 abbreviates the fully specified map (x,z,τ)↦gj,0​(x,hj,0​(z0),zc,τ)(x,z,\tau)\mapsto g_{j,0}(x,h_{j,0}(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau). Only the source part of Assumption 2 is needed for the transfer source rate. The target part is needed for the target-only theorem.

Assumption 3 (Calibrated source representations and reduced-mean regularity).

Fix rt>1r_{t}>1, Bg,t<∞B_{g,t}<\infty, and positive margins ηx,t,ηu,t,ητ,t\eta_{x,t},\eta_{u,t},\eta_{\tau,t}. There are a deterministic measurable set ℋgood\mathcal{H}_{\rm good}, constants κ≥0\kappa\geq 0, Δ≥0\Delta\geq 0, and a deterministic number πs∈[0,1]\pi_{s}\in[0,1] such that ℙ⁡(h^s∉ℋgood)≤πs\mathbb{P}(\widehat{h}_{s}\notin\mathcal{H}_{\rm good})\leq\pi_{s}. For every h∈ℋgoodh\in\mathcal{H}_{\rm good},

𝒟t​(h)≤κ​𝒟s​(h)+Δ2.\mathcal{D}_{t}(h)\leq\kappa\mathcal{D}_{s}(h)+\Delta^{2}. (3.3)

Also, the reduced conditional mean in Equation 2.9 has a version gt,h∈Crt​(𝒦t,Bg,t)g_{t,h}\in C^{r_{t}}(\mathcal{K}_{t};B_{g,t}), taking values in [−bt,bt]dt[-b_{t},b_{t}]^{d_{t}}, with

uniformly in hh. The constants are independent of sample sizes.

3.2 Frozen neural transfer

Theorem 1 (End-to-end neural bound for TFM-Freeze).

Use Section 2.4 with Equation 3.6. Suppose Assumption 1, the source part of Assumption 2, and Assumption 3 hold. Then

𝔼​𝒟s​(h^s)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{D}_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s}) ≤C​Rs​(ns),\displaystyle\leq CR_{s}(n_{s}), (3.9)
𝔼​ℰt​(F^F)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{F}) ≤C⁡{ρrt,Dt​(nt)+Ts​(ns)},\displaystyle\leq C\{\rho_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t})+T_{s}(n_{s})\}, (3.10)
𝔼​𝒲t2​(PF^F[J],Pt0)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{W}_{t}^{2}(P_{\widehat{F}_{F}}^{[J]},P_{t}^{0}) ≤C⁡{ρrt,Dt​(nt)+Ts​(ns)+J−2}.\displaystyle\leq C\{\rho_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t})+T_{s}(n_{s})+J^{-2}\}. (3.11)

For exact ODE integration, omit J−2J^{-2}. In the exact, globally calibrated case ζs=Δ=πs=0\zeta_{s}=\Delta=\pi_{s}=0, the bound is

C⁡{(ℓnt3nt)2​rt/(2​rt+Dt)+κ​(ℓns3ns)2​rs/(2​rs+Ds)+κ​(ℓns3ns)2​βs/(2​βs+p)+J−2}.C\left\{\left(\frac{\ell_{n_{t}}^{3}}{n_{t}}\right)^{\!2r_{t}/(2r_{t}+D_{t})}+\kappa\left(\frac{\ell_{n_{s}}^{3}}{n_{s}}\right)^{\!2r_{s}/(2r_{s}+D_{s})}+\kappa\left(\frac{\ell_{n_{s}}^{3}}{n_{s}}\right)^{\!2\beta_{s}/(2\beta_{s}+p)}+J^{-2}\right\}. (3.12)

Proof. Appendix C.

The target fit pays only for a reduced-input neural head. The source contribution is derived from joint neural source regression, including its head and representation complexities. Projection and calibration transfer this bound to the target; ODE stability and the Euler bound complete the generation analysis. This is the main guarantee for Algorithm 2.4.

3.3 Functionally anchored neural adaptation

We analyze an explicit neural function class and compare the two training algorithms under the same correctability condition.

Let 𝒮=σ⁡(𝒟s,source auxiliary draws,𝒟a)\mathscr{S}=\sigma(\mathscr{D}_{s},\text{source auxiliary draws},\mathscr{D}_{a}), which is independent of target training, and put Kt=BU,t+BV,tK_{t}=B_{U,t}+B_{V,t}. Fix a nonempty coordinate set IA⊆{1,…,p}I_{A}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}, write qA=|IA|q_{A}=|I_{A}|, and let z0,IA∈[−1,1]qAz_{0,I_{A}}\in[-1,1]^{q_{A}} be the selected common-context coordinates. For a fixed BR>0B_{R}>0, define the residual neural sieve and the source-conditioned encoder class by

ℛA,M\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{A,M} ={a=clipBR⁡f∘Π[−1,1]qA:f∈𝒩qA,dh​(M)},\displaystyle=\{a=\operatorname{clip}_{B_{R}}f\circ\Pi_{[-1,1]^{q_{A}}}:f\in\mathcal{N}_{q_{A},d_{h}}(M)\}, (3.13)

The zero residual belongs to ℛA,M\mathcal{R}_{A,M}, so h^s∈ℋA​(M)\widehat{h}_{s}\in\mathcal{H}_{A}(M). The sum, the two clipping maps, and the parallel branches in Equation 3.14 are ReLU implementations. The source branch stays fixed, but the residual network aa and target head vv are fitted jointly. The residual can use coordinates missing from h^s\widehat{h}_{s}. Restricting every updated encoder to be a function of h^s\widehat{h}_{s} alone would not recover such missing information.

The mean empirical anchor in Equation 2.18, on any declared finite design, and the supremum anchor in Equation 2.19 satisfy

0≤As​(hh^s,a)≤‖a‖∞2,As​(h^s)=0.0\leq A_{s}(h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a})\leq\|a\|_{\infty}^{2},\qquad A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s})=0. (3.15)

Indeed, output clipping fixes h^s\widehat{h}_{s} and is nonexpansive. Any other nonnegative, target-independent functional anchor satisfying Equation 3.15 is also permitted here.

+κA[ζs2+ρrs,Ds(ns)+ρβs,p(ns)]}.\displaystyle+\kappa_{A}[\zeta_{s}^{2}+\rho_{r_{s},D_{s}}(n_{s})+\rho_{\beta_{s},p}(n_{s})]\big\}.

Adaptation replaces the frozen correction-size contribution Lu,t2​δA2L_{u,t}^{2}\delta_{A}^{2} by a learned residual contribution ρβA,qA​(nt)+λ​δA2\rho_{\beta_{A},q_{A}}(n_{t})+\lambda\delta_{A}^{2}. The frozen comparison is proved under the same conditions.

The range in Equation 3.24 includes λnt=0\lambda_{n_{t}}=0 at every sample size. A zero penalty removes the contribution λnt​δA2\lambda_{n_{t}}\delta_{A}^{2}, but not the residual-learning term ρβA,qA​(nt)\rho_{\beta_{A},q_{A}}(n_{t}).

3.4 When the advantage is an actual risk separation

We next give a separate, checkable information-loss condition that orders actual risks. Let μt​(z)=𝔼⁡(Xt∣Zt=z)\mu_{t}(z)=\mathbb{E}(X_{t}\mid Z_{t}=z), and, for a fixed representation hh, define

A non-transfer estimator uses only 𝒟t\mathscr{D}_{t} and its auxiliary draws. Set Mt=Kβt,p​(nt)M_{t}=K_{\beta_{t},p}(n_{t}), use the same target head resolution Nt=Krt,Dt​(nt)N_{t}=K_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t}), and define

This is a separately trained target-only estimator. It does not use a source initialization, a source representation, or a source-based anchor.

4 Endpoint validation and target-only safeguards

In this section, we present the procedure to prevent negative transfer. Before fitting candidates, split the target sample into independent parts 𝒟tr\mathscr{D}_{\rm tr} and 𝒟val\mathscr{D}_{\rm val}, of sizes ntrn_{\rm tr} and nvaln_{\rm val}. Train candidates with nt=ntrn_{t}=n_{\rm tr}, including architecture and tolerance choices. The validation observations and simulation draws are excluded from representation learning, anchor construction, fitting, and dictionary construction.

Condition on the pre-validation information 𝒮tr\mathscr{S}_{\rm tr}, fixing ℱ=(F1,…,FM)\mathscr{F}=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{M}) with deterministic M≥2M\geq 2. Include the target-only candidate FNTF_{\rm NT} trained on ntrn_{\rm tr} observations. Other entries may be frozen fits, adaptive fits at predeclared nonnegative penalties λ\lambda, possibly including zero, or fits using different declared architectures. All fields satisfy the common target envelopes and state/time Lipschitz bounds in Equation 2.15.

4.1 Endpoint laws, conditional scores, and the validation experiment

We validate the deployed endpoint laws. Throughout the rest of this section write n=nvaln=n_{\rm val}, d=dtd=d_{t}, and

Pz=Pt0(⋅∣z),Qm,z=PFm[Jm](⋅∣z),1≤m≤M.P_{z}=P_{t}^{0}(\cdot\mid z),\qquad Q_{m,z}=P_{F_{m}}^{[J_{m}]}(\cdot\mid z),\quad 1\leq m\leq M. (4.1)

Exact integration is also allowed. Each solver and its resolution JmJ_{m} are fixed as part of the pre-validation candidate. The notation Qm=(Qm,z)zQ_{m}=(Q_{m,z})_{z} denotes a probability kernel, and m0m_{0} indexes the included target-only kernel QNT=Qm0Q_{\rm NT}=Q_{m_{0}}. Conditionally on 𝒮tr\mathscr{S}_{\rm tr}, these kernels are fixed. Endpoint validation uses the original pairs (Xi,Zi)∼iidPt0(X_{i},Z_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm iid}}{{\sim}}P_{t}^{0}. Generated endpoints used to approximate a score are auxiliary randomness; they do not increase the number nn of target observations.

Assumption 5 (Common bounded endpoint support).

There is a fixed compact set 𝒦e⊂ℝd\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} of Euclidean diameter at most De>0D_{\rm e}>0 such that, for target-almost every zz, PzP_{z} and every Qm,zQ_{m,z} are supported on 𝒦e\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}. All kernels and sampling maps are measurable. The validation sample is independent of 𝒮tr\mathscr{S}_{\rm tr}.

This is sufficient for the distribution-free bounded-score statements below; it does not require calibration, correctability, or a correct flow-matching model. It is available in the paper’s regime. Indeed, absolute continuity of the interpolation paths and Assumption 1 imply that Gt,XtG_{t},X_{t} lie in [−Kx,t,Kx,t]d[-K_{x,t},K_{x,t}]^{d} almost surely. A field bounded by BV,tB_{V,t} moves its initial point by at most BV,tB_{V,t}, for both exact and Euler integration. Thus one may take 𝒦e=[−Kx,t−BV,t,Kx,t+BV,t]d\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}=[-K_{x,t}-B_{V,t},K_{x,t}+B_{V,t}]^{d}. Lemma E.1 supplies the endpoint and solver details.

Fix an energy exponent υ∈(0,2)\upsilon\in(0,2), usually υ=1\upsilon=1, and set Ae=DeυA_{\rm e}=D_{\rm e}^{\upsilon}. Define the negatively oriented energy score and energy discrepancy by

Sυ​(Q,x)\displaystyle S_{\upsilon}(Q,x) =𝔼Y∼Q​‖Y−x‖υ−12​𝔼Y,Y′∼iidQ​‖Y−Y′‖υ,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim Q}\|Y-x\|^{\upsilon}-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{Y,Y^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm iid}}{{\sim}}Q}\|Y-Y^{\prime}\|^{\upsilon}, (4.2)
𝖣υ​(P,Q)\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{\upsilon}(P,Q) =2​𝔼​‖X−Y‖υ−𝔼​‖X−X′‖υ−𝔼​‖Y−Y′‖υ,\displaystyle=2\mathbb{E}\|X-Y\|^{\upsilon}-\mathbb{E}\|X-X^{\prime}\|^{\upsilon}-\mathbb{E}\|Y-Y^{\prime}\|^{\upsilon}, (4.3)
ℛE,υ​(Q)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{{\rm E},\upsilon}(Q) =12​𝔼Zt​𝖣υ​(PZt,QZt).\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}}\mathsf{D}_{\upsilon}(P_{Z_{t}},Q_{Z_{t}}). (4.4)

The four variables in Equation 4.3 are independent, with X,X′∼PX,X^{\prime}\sim P and Y,Y′∼QY,Y^{\prime}\sim Q. Lower scores are better. We use 𝖣υ\mathsf{D}_{\upsilon} for the conventional energy discrepancy. Most importantly,

𝔼​Sυ​(QZt,Xt)−𝔼​Sυ​(PZt,Xt)=ℛE,υ​(Q)≥0,\mathbb{E}S_{\upsilon}(Q_{Z_{t}},X_{t})-\mathbb{E}S_{\upsilon}(P_{Z_{t}},X_{t})=\mathcal{R}_{{\rm E},\upsilon}(Q)\geq 0, (4.5)

with equality exactly when Qz=PzQ_{z}=P_{z} for target-almost every zz. The unknown second term is common to all candidates and need not be estimated. Thus one observed endpoint per context suffices for conditional energy-score validation, even when the contexts are continuously distributed. The underlying proper-score and Hilbert-space identities are classical (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007; Sejdinovic et al., 2013); Lemma E.3 gives a self-contained proof with the normalization used here.

At validation context ZiZ_{i}, simulate B≥2B\geq 2 endpoints for each candidate mm. Conditionally on the validation pair and fitted dictionary, these draws are independent with Ym,i,1,…,Ym,i,B∼Qm,ZiY_{m,i,1},\ldots,Y_{m,i,B}\sim Q_{m,Z_{i}}. Use the unbiased score

Under Assumption 5 and the simulation scheme above, conditionally on 𝒮tr\mathscr{S}_{\rm tr}, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over validation and simulation, all of the following hold:

ℛE,υ​(Qm^E)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{{\rm E},\upsilon}(Q_{\widehat{m}_{\rm E}}) ≤minm⁡ℛE,υ​(Qm)+2​εE​(δ),\displaystyle\leq\min_{m}\mathcal{R}_{{\rm E},\upsilon}(Q_{m})+2\varepsilon_{\rm E}(\delta), (4.9)

On the same high-probability event, if the best candidate improves on QNTQ_{\rm NT} in this risk by more than 4​εE​(δ)4\varepsilon_{\rm E}(\delta), the safe rule switches.

Proof. Appendix E.

Note that this is a leading-constant-one oracle for a deployed endpoint generator. The conservative version has no deterioration relative to the actual target-only endpoint law on its confidence event, in the declared energy risk. Fixed B≥2B\geq 2 suffices for consistency of finite-dictionary selection: the Monte Carlo score is unbiased and its rows are independent. No target conditional-density estimator is required.

5 Simulation studies

We investigate the accuracy gained by adapting a source representation and the ability of target validation to guard against negative transfer. The design varies the source sample size and the discrepancy between the source and target representations, while keeping the target sample size fixed. It includes nonlinear sufficient representations, heteroscedastic responses, and a target conditional distribution with two mixture components.

5.1 Data-generating process

In each domain, let Z∼Np​(0,Ip)Z\sim N_{p}(0,I_{p}), with independent observations across and within domains. Fix p×4p\times 4 matrices BB and CC such that [B,C][B,C] has orthonormal columns, and set Bs=BB_{s}=B and Bt=cos⁡(θ)​B+sin⁡(θ)​CB_{t}=\cos(\theta)B+\sin(\theta)C. All errors ϵj,k\epsilon_{j,k} are independent standard normal variables, independent of the covariates and mixture labels. The label LL is shared across target response coordinates and induces conditional dependence when d>1d>1. Thus the source and target response laws differ even when their representations are closely related. The projection matrices, representations, and mixture parameters are not supplied to the fitted procedures.

The dimension pairs are (p,d)=(50,1)(p,d)=(50,1), (200,5)(200,5), and (500,10)(500,10). We fix nt=1024n_{t}=1024 and take ns=1000n_{s}=1000, 20002000, 40004000, or 80008000. Each setting has 100 independent training repetitions. Within a repetition, the methods share the same observations and evaluation samples.

5.2 Methods and evaluation

We compare target-only diffusion, target-only flow matching (FM), the frozen-representation diffusion construction of Tian and Shen (2026), TFM-Freeze, TFM-Adapt, and TFM-Adapt with λ=0\lambda=0. The positive-penalty procedure selects λ∈{0.01,0.1,1}\lambda\in\{0.01,0.1,1\} by tuning; the unpenalized procedure fixes λ=0\lambda=0. We also apply a target-validation safeguard to each of the three TFM procedures, giving nine methods in total. These versions are denoted by +TV+\mathrm{TV}. They compare a tuned transfer candidate with target-only FM on separate target observations and select the target-only fit when the validation evidence does not favor transfer. The common neural architecture, tuning protocol, and validation rule are given in Section F.1. Accuracy is measured by the context-averaged energy discrepancy and joint empirical Wasserstein distances W1W_{1} and W2W_{2}. Lower values indicate more accurate generation. Evaluation details and uncertainty calculations are given in Section F.3.

5.3 Generation accuracy and negative transfer

Figure 1 shows substantial gains from adaptation in the related setting. For d=1d=1 and d=5d=5, both adaptive procedures have smaller mean energy discrepancy than the frozen and target-only alternatives throughout the source-size grid. At ns=8000n_{s}=8000, the unpenalized procedure attains 0.2325 for d=1d=1, compared with 0.3158 for TFM-Freeze, the strongest nonadaptive comparator, a reduction of 26.4%. For d=5d=5, TFM-Adapt reduces the discrepancy from 0.2589 to 0.2118, an improvement of 18.2%. Paired comparisons support both adaptive procedures over all five nonadaptive comparators in these two dimensions (Section F.4).

Figures 2 and 3 corroborate the adaptation gains for d=1d=1 and d=5d=5 under both Wasserstein criteria. The ten-dimensional setting also benefits from transfer: TFM-Adapt reduces energy discrepancy by 37.9% relative to target-only FM at ns=8000n_{s}=8000, with TFM-Freeze attaining the smallest discrepancy in that setting. The similar performance of positive and zero penalties in the first two dimensions indicates that allowing the representation to adapt is an important source of the observed gain.

The right panels examine unrelated representations. With target validation, each adaptive procedure has at most one harmful repetition out of 100 in every setting, and none at ns=8000n_{s}=8000. At that source size, both recover target-only FM exactly in all three dimensions. For related five-dimensional responses at the same source size, validation retains both adaptive fits in all 100 repetitions. Thus the safeguard preserves the accuracy gain when transfer is useful in this setting and returns to target-only learning when the representations are unrelated. Counts use energy discrepancy; Table 2 gives the comparisons with and without validation.

6 Real-data applications

We consider Materials and Diamonds, two conditional distribution prediction problems with different source and target populations. The same nine procedures are compared. Each application uses 40 paired training repetitions. We assess prediction by the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) on held-out target observations; lower values are better. Here, CRPS is the energy score with exponent one (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Data construction and uncertainty calculations are described in Sections F.2 and F.3.

6.1 Superconducting materials

The Materials application uses the UCI superconductivity data (Hamidieh, 2018). The response is log⁡(1+Tc)\log(1+T_{c}), where TcT_{c} is the critical temperature in kelvin, and the predictors are 81 chemical descriptors. Copper-oxide compounds without iron form the source domain; iron-bearing compounds without copper form the target domain. Each repetition uses ns=6000n_{s}=6000 source and nt=256n_{t}=256 target compositions, with 336 target compositions reserved for testing.

This application illustrates the protection provided by target validation. Both adaptive procedures with validation attain mean CRPS 0.31826, equal to target-only FM, with zero harmful repetitions out of 40 (Table 1). In every repetition, the safeguard selects the target-only fit. It thereby avoids the loss incurred by transferring between these populations: without validation, TFM-Adapt and its λ=0\lambda=0 version have mean CRPS 0.35067 and 0.34833. The gain here is preservation of target-only FM performance through a data-dependent decision about whether to transfer.

6.2 Diamond prices

The Diamonds application predicts log price from 19 variables describing carat, depth and table percentages, physical dimensions, color, and clarity (ggplot2 authors, n.d.). Premium and Very Good cuts form the source domain, and Ideal cuts form the target domain. Cut grade is excluded from the predictors. Each repetition uses ns=12000n_{s}=12000 source and nt=2048n_{t}=2048 target groups, with 1024 target groups reserved for testing.

Table 1 shows that adaptation improves prediction in this application. TFM-Adapt attains the lowest mean CRPS, 0.06357, followed closely by its λ=0\lambda=0 version at 0.06365. These values improve on target-only FM by 8.05% and 7.95%, respectively, and on TFM-Freeze by 3.65% and 3.54%. Pointwise 95% paired Student-tt intervals favor both adaptive procedures over each of the five nonadaptive comparators (Table 3). TFM-Adapt improves on target-only FM in all 40 repetitions. Its validated version retains transfer in 39 repetitions, has zero harmful repetitions, and attains CRPS 0.06371. Thus target validation preserves most of the adaptation gain on Diamonds while recovering target-only performance on Materials.

A.1 Conditional regression and the probability path

Lemma A.1 (Orthogonal decomposition and deficiency).

Under the moment condition in Equation 2.2, every square-integrable field F=Fj,v,hF=F_{j,v,h} satisfies Equation 2.11 and ℒj​(v,h)−ℒj∗=ℰj​(F)\mathcal{L}_{j}(v,h)-\mathcal{L}_{j}^{*}=\mathcal{E}_{j}(F). Moreover,

𝔼⁡⟨F−v0,v0−U⟩=𝔼⁡⟨F−v0,𝔼⁡(v0−U∣W)⟩=0.\mathbb{E}\langle F-v^{0},v^{0}-U\rangle=\mathbb{E}\langle F-v^{0},\mathbb{E}(v^{0}-U\mid W)\rangle=0.

Expanding F−U=(F−v0)+(v0−U)F-U=(F-v^{0})+(v^{0}-U) proves the excess-risk identity. Let ℬh=σ⁡(Sj,T,Hj,h​(Zj),T)\mathcal{B}_{h}=\sigma(S_{j,T},H_{j,h}(Z_{j}),T). The tower property gives 𝔼⁡(v0∣ℬh)=m\mathbb{E}(v^{0}\mid\mathcal{B}_{h})=m, so

Lemma A.2 (Conditional marginal-flow identity).

Under Equation 2.2, the conditional interpolation laws satisfy the weak continuity equation with velocity vj0v_{j}^{0} given ZjZ_{j}, and with velocity mj,hm_{j,h} given the reduced context Hj,h​(Zj)H_{j,h}(Z_{j}). A reduced-context characteristic has endpoint law Pj0(⋅∣Hj,h(Zj))P_{j}^{0}(\cdot\mid H_{j,h}(Z_{j})) only when the analogous reduced-context realization and uniqueness also hold.

Let φ\varphi be a continuously differentiable compactly supported function on ℝdj\mathbb{R}^{d_{j}}, and let 0≤a<b≤10\leq a<b\leq 1. The chain rule along the almost surely absolutely continuous path gives

φ(Sj,b)−φ(Sj,a)=∫ab∇φ(Sj,u)⊤Uj,udu.\varphi(S_{j,b})-\varphi(S_{j,a})=\int_{a}^{b}\nabla\varphi(S_{j,u})^{\top}U_{j,u}\,\mathrm{d}u.

The integrand is absolutely integrable in expectation, because ‖∇φ‖∞<∞\|\nabla\varphi\|_{\infty}<\infty and 𝔼​∫01‖Uj,u‖​𝑑u<∞\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{1}\|U_{j,u}\|\,\mathrm{d}u<\infty by Cauchy–Schwarz. For almost every uu, this replaces Uj,uU_{j,u} by vj0​(Sj,u,Zj,u)v_{j}^{0}(S_{j,u},Z_{j},u), yielding

𝔼{φ(Sj,b)−φ(Sj,a)∣Zj}=∫ab𝔼{∇φ(Sj,u)⊤vj0(Sj,u,Zj,u)∣Zj}du.\mathbb{E}\{\varphi(S_{j,b})-\varphi(S_{j,a})\mid Z_{j}\}=\int_{a}^{b}\mathbb{E}\{\nabla\varphi(S_{j,u})^{\top}v_{j}^{0}(S_{j,u},Z_{j},u)\mid Z_{j}\}\,\mathrm{d}u.

This is the integrated weak continuity equation. Conditioning instead on Hj,h​(Zj)H_{j,h}(Z_{j}) gives the reduced version with mj,hm_{j,h}. The endpoint identities follow from Sj,0=GjS_{j,0}=G_{j}, Sj,1=XjS_{j,1}=X_{j}, and the respective characteristic realization assumptions. ∎

B.1 A multiplication module

Lemma B.1 (Multiplication with a Lipschitz-small error).

Fix A≥1A\geq 1. For every 0<δ<1/20<\delta<1/2 there is a ReLU network Pδ,A:ℝ2→ℝP_{\delta,A}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} such that, on [−A,A]2[-A,A]^{2},

‖Pδ,A​(a,b)−a​b‖∞≤δ,Lip⁡(Pδ,A​(a,b)−a​b)≤δ.\|P_{\delta,A}(a,b)-ab\|_{\infty}\leq\delta,\qquad\operatorname{Lip}(P_{\delta,A}(a,b)-ab)\leq\delta. (B.1)

Moreover Pδ,A​(a,0)=Pδ,A​(0,b)=0P_{\delta,A}(a,0)=P_{\delta,A}(0,b)=0 exactly on this box. Its width is bounded by a constant depending on AA, its depth and number of nonzero parameters are at most CA​log⁡(1/δ)C_{A}\log(1/\delta), and its parameter magnitudes are bounded by a constant depending on AA.

Proof.

On [0,1][0,1], let T⁡(u)=2​ReLU⁡(u)−4​ReLU⁡(u−1/2)+2​ReLU⁡(u−1)T(u)=2\operatorname{ReLU}(u)-4\operatorname{ReLU}(u-1/2)+2\operatorname{ReLU}(u-1), and let TjT_{j} denote its jj-fold composition. The function

Sq​(u)=u−∑j=1q4−j​Tj​(u)S_{q}(u)=u-\sum_{j=1}^{q}4^{-j}T_{j}(u)

is the piecewise-linear interpolant of u2u^{2} on the mesh of spacing 2−q2^{-q}. To check this, start with the chord S0​(u)=uS_{0}(u)=u. On each old mesh interval the next tent is zero at both endpoints and one at the midpoint, and subtracting 4−(q+1)4^{-(q+1)} gives the exact midpoint value of the quadratic. Both sides are affine on the new half intervals, completing the induction. On an interval [a,a+h][a,a+h] with h=2−qh=2^{-q}, the interpolation error is (u−a)​(a+h−u)(u-a)(a+h-u). Consequently

‖Sq−u2‖∞≤h2/4,Lip⁡(Sq−u2)≤h.\|S_{q}-u^{2}\|_{\infty}\leq h^{2}/4,\qquad\operatorname{Lip}(S_{q}-u^{2})\leq h.

Set A∗=2​AA_{*}=2A, and define qq​(z)=A∗2​Sq​(|z|/A∗)q_{q}(z)=A_{*}^{2}S_{q}(|z|/A_{*}) for |z|≤A∗|z|\leq A_{*}. The function qqq_{q} is even, and its error from z2z^{2} has supremum norm at most A∗2​h2/4A_{*}^{2}h^{2}/4 and Lipschitz constant at most A∗​hA_{*}h. Polarization gives

Pδ,A​(a,b)=14​{qq​(a+b)−qq​(a−b)}.P_{\delta,A}(a,b)=\tfrac{1}{4}\{q_{q}(a+b)-q_{q}(a-b)\}.

The value error is at most A∗2​h2/8A_{*}^{2}h^{2}/8. Since each of the linear maps (a,b)↦a±b(a,b)\mapsto a\pm b has Euclidean operator norm 2\sqrt{2}, the Lipschitz constant of the error is at most A∗​h/2A_{*}h/\sqrt{2}. Choose qq so that these two bounds are at most δ\delta. Evenness gives the exact zero assertions.

The recursion for TjT_{j}, together with a running partial sum, uses constant width and O⁡(q)O(q) layers and parameters. Signed registers are represented by their positive and negative parts if required by the ReLU layers. Its coefficients, including 4−j4^{-j}, are uniformly bounded; the affine rescalings depend only on AA. As q≤CA​log⁡(1/δ)q\leq C_{A}\log(1/\delta), the architecture bounds follow. ∎

For arbitrary q,q′∈Kq,q^{\prime}\in K, fix q∘∈int⁡Kq_{\circ}\in\operatorname{int}K and apply the interior inequality to q(t)=(1−t)​q+t​q∘q^{(t)}=(1-t)q+tq_{\circ} and q′(t)=(1−t)​q′+t​q∘q^{\prime(t)}=(1-t)q^{\prime}+tq_{\circ}, where 0<t<10<t<1. Proposition B.3 (Finite cell-slope characterization).

A finite ReLU network with the declared input and output clips is continuous and piecewise affine on a finite polyhedral partition. On each full-dimensional cell CC, write its head as v⁡(q)=AC​q+bCv(q)=A_{C}q+b_{C}. For a block b∈{x,u,τ}b\in\{x,u,\tau\}, let AC,bA_{C,b} be the corresponding columns. On the full input space,

Lipb⁡(v)=maxC​ full-dimensional⁡‖AC,b‖op.\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(v)=\max_{C\text{ full-dimensional}}\|A_{C,b}\|_{\rm op}. (B.50)

Thus the actual constraints in Equation 2.15 have a finite exact characterization, although enumerating the cells may be expensive.

Proof.

Write v:ℝD→ℝmv:\mathbb{R}^{D}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} for the head including its declared input projection and output clipping. For the head sieve 𝒱j,N\mathcal{V}_{j,N}, the dimensions are D=DjD=D_{j} and m=djm=d_{j}, with DjD_{j} as in Equation (2.14). Fix a block b∈{x,u,τ}b\in\{x,u,\tau\} of dimension dbd_{b}, and let Jb:ℝdb→ℝDJ_{b}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{b}}\to\mathbb{R}^{D} be the coordinate insertion map defined in Equation (B.42). In particular, ‖Jb​w‖=‖w‖\|J_{b}w\|=\|w\|. The definition on the full input space is

Lipb⁡(v)=supq∈ℝDw∈ℝdb∖{0}‖v⁡(q+Jb​w)−v⁡(q)‖‖w‖.\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(v)=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\\ w\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{b}}\setminus\{0\}\end{subarray}}\frac{\|v(q+J_{b}w)-v(q)\|}{\|w\|}. (B.51)

The matrix of block columns in the proposition is AC,b=AC​JbA_{C,b}=A_{C}J_{b}.

Step 1: A finite affine representation on polyhedral cells. Let ϱ⁡(s)=max⁡(s,0)\varrho(s)=\max(s,0). For any interval [ℓ,r][\ell,r], scalar coordinate clipping has the exact representation

clip[ℓ,r]⁡(s)=ℓ+ϱ⁡(s−ℓ)−ϱ⁡(s−r).\operatorname{clip}_{[\ell,r]}(s)=\ell+\varrho(s-\ell)-\varrho(s-r). (B.52)

Thus each coordinate of the input projection and the output clipping is itself a finite ReLU realization. Absorbing these operations into a finite network, write its hidden-layer computation as

z(0)​(q)\displaystyle z^{(0)}(q) =q,\displaystyle=q, (B.53)
u(ℓ)​(q)\displaystyle u^{(\ell)}(q) =Wℓ​z(ℓ−1)​(q)+cℓ,\displaystyle=W_{\ell}z^{(\ell-1)}(q)+c_{\ell}, z(ℓ)​(q)\displaystyle z^{(\ell)}(q) =ϱ(u(ℓ)(q)),1≤ℓ≤L,\displaystyle=\varrho(u^{(\ell)}(q)),\quad 1\leq\ell\leq L,
v⁡(q)\displaystyle v(q) =WL+1​z(L)​(q)+cL+1.\displaystyle=W_{L+1}z^{(L)}(q)+c_{L+1}.

Here LL is the finite hidden-layer count, nℓn_{\ell} is the width of layer ℓ\ell, WℓW_{\ell} is its weight matrix, and cℓc_{\ell} is its bias vector. All affine maps and all coordinatewise ReLU maps in Equation (B.53) are continuous; therefore their composition vv is continuous on ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}.

An activation pattern is a collection ω=(ω1,…,ωL)\omega=(\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{L}), with ωℓ∈{0,1}nℓ\omega_{\ell}\in\{0,1\}^{n_{\ell}}. Define its diagonal gate matrix Γω,ℓ=diag⁡(ωℓ)\Gamma_{\omega,\ell}=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_{\ell}). For this pattern, set Aω,0=IDA_{\omega,0}=I_{D}, bω,0=0b_{\omega,0}=0, and recursively define

Bω,ℓ\displaystyle B_{\omega,\ell} =Wℓ​Aω,ℓ−1,\displaystyle=W_{\ell}A_{\omega,\ell-1}, dω,ℓ\displaystyle d_{\omega,\ell} =Wℓ​bω,ℓ−1+cℓ,\displaystyle=W_{\ell}b_{\omega,\ell-1}+c_{\ell}, (B.54)
Aω,ℓ\displaystyle A_{\omega,\ell} =Γω,ℓ​Bω,ℓ,\displaystyle=\Gamma_{\omega,\ell}B_{\omega,\ell}, bω,ℓ\displaystyle b_{\omega,\ell} =Γω,ℓ​dω,ℓ.\displaystyle=\Gamma_{\omega,\ell}d_{\omega,\ell}.

The consistency region for the activation pattern ω\omega is

Cω=⋂ℓ=1L⋂r=1nℓ{q∈ℝD:(2​ωℓ,r−1)​[Bω,ℓ​q+dω,ℓ]r≥0}.C_{\omega}=\bigcap_{\ell=1}^{L}\bigcap_{r=1}^{n_{\ell}}\left\{q\in\mathbb{R}^{D}:(2\omega_{\ell,r}-1)[B_{\omega,\ell}q+d_{\omega,\ell}]_{r}\geq 0\right\}. (B.55)

Every set in this intersection is a closed half-space, the whole space, or the empty set. Hence CωC_{\omega} is a closed convex polyhedron, possibly empty or lower-dimensional. If q∈Cωq\in C_{\omega}, induction over ℓ\ell using Equations (B.53) and (B.55) proves z(ℓ)​(q)=Aω,ℓ​q+bω,ℓz^{(\ell)}(q)=A_{\omega,\ell}q+b_{\omega,\ell}. This remains true for zero preactivations, because both choices of a gate on a zero coordinate produce zero. Consequently,

v⁡(q)=Aω​q+bω(q∈Cω),{Aω=WL+1​Aω,L,bω=WL+1​bω,L+cL+1.v(q)=A_{\omega}q+b_{\omega}\quad(q\in C_{\omega}),\qquad\begin{cases}A_{\omega}=W_{L+1}A_{\omega,L},\\ b_{\omega}=W_{L+1}b_{\omega,L}+c_{L+1}.\end{cases} (B.56)

There are at most 2∑ℓ=1Lnℓ2^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}n_{\ell}} activation patterns, and their regions CωC_{\omega} cover ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}, because the actual preactivation signs at every input qq provide a consistent pattern.

To obtain a partition with disjoint interiors, collect the finitely many hyperplanes defined by all nonconstant affine expressions in Equation (B.55). Constant affine expressions need not be included: a nonzero constant has a fixed sign, and an identically zero expression imposes no sign restriction. The nonempty open cells of this finite hyperplane arrangement are intersections of strict half-spaces and therefore are convex and full-dimensional. On an open cell, every relevant affine expression has a fixed sign, so that cell lies in at least one region CωC_{\omega}; Equation (B.56) then gives one affine formula for vv on the cell. If two patterns are consistent there, their affine formulas agree on an open set and hence have identical coefficients.

Let 𝒞\mathscr{C} be the finite collection of closures of these nonempty open cells. Every C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C} is a closed, full-dimensional convex polyhedron. Their union is ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}: the complement of the finitely many hyperplanes is dense, and any convergent sequence in that complement has a subsequence lying in one of its finitely many cells. Continuity of vv extends each affine formula to the cell closure, giving

⋃C∈𝒞C=ℝD,v(q)=ACq+bC(q∈C).\bigcup_{C\in\mathscr{C}}C=\mathbb{R}^{D},\qquad v(q)=A_{C}q+b_{C}\quad(q\in C). (B.57)

If the hyperplane collection is empty, take 𝒞={ℝD}\mathscr{C}=\{\mathbb{R}^{D}\}. The cell closures and their faces give a finite polyhedral partition in the usual sense. Subdividing an already affine cell does not change its matrix ACA_{C}, and therefore does not change the maximum of the block operator norms.

Lb∗=maxC∈𝒞⁡‖AC​Jb‖op.L_{b}^{*}=\max_{C\in\mathscr{C}}\|A_{C}J_{b}\|_{\rm op}. (B.58)

Fix an arbitrary input q∈ℝDq\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and a nonzero block increment w∈ℝdbw\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{b}}, and parameterize their segment by

q⁡(t)=q+t​Jb​w,0≤t≤1.q(t)=q+tJ_{b}w,\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1. (B.59)

0=t0<t1<⋯<tJ=1.0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{J}=1. (B.60)

For each j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,J, choose a cell Cj∈𝒞C_{j}\in\mathscr{C} whose interval ICjI_{C_{j}} contains the midpoint of (tj−1,tj)(t_{j-1},t_{j}). No endpoint of ICjI_{C_{j}} can lie strictly between tj−1t_{j-1} and tjt_{j}, by the definition of Equation (B.60). Since ICjI_{C_{j}} is closed, it follows that

[tj−1,tj]⊂ICj,q⁡([tj−1,tj])⊂Cj.[t_{j-1},t_{j}]\subset I_{C_{j}},\qquad q([t_{j-1},t_{j}])\subset C_{j}. (B.61)

This argument does not require a transverse crossing of cell boundaries. It applies even when the entire segment q⁡([0,1])q([0,1]) lies in a lower-dimensional face, because Equation (B.57) is valid on the closed full-dimensional cells containing that face.

Step 3: The upper bound Lipb⁡(v)≤Lb∗\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(v)\leq L_{b}^{*}. Equations (B.57) and (B.61) give the exact increment identity

=(tj−tj−1)​ACj​Jb​w.\displaystyle=(t_{j}-t_{j-1})A_{C_{j}}J_{b}w.

Summing Equation (B.62) telescopically, then applying the triangle inequality and the definition of an operator norm, yields

‖v⁡(q+Jb​w)−v⁡(q)‖\displaystyle\|v(q+J_{b}w)-v(q)\| =‖∑j=1J(tj−tj−1)​ACj​Jb​w‖\displaystyle=\left\|\sum_{j=1}^{J}(t_{j}-t_{j-1})A_{C_{j}}J_{b}w\right\|
≤∑j=1J(tj−tj−1)​‖ACj​Jb‖op​‖w‖\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{J}(t_{j}-t_{j-1})\|A_{C_{j}}J_{b}\|_{\rm op}\|w\|
≤Lb∗​‖w‖​∑j=1J(tj−tj−1)=Lb∗​‖w‖.\displaystyle\leq L_{b}^{*}\|w\|\sum_{j=1}^{J}(t_{j}-t_{j-1})=L_{b}^{*}\|w\|. (B.63)

Taking the supremum over q,wq,w in Equation (B.51) proves Lipb⁡(v)≤Lb∗\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(v)\leq L_{b}^{*}. In particular, this argument proves the bound for every segment, not merely for almost every segment.

Step 4: The lower bound Lipb⁡(v)≥Lb∗\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(v)\geq L_{b}^{*}. Fix any full-dimensional cell C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C}. Choose qC∈int⁡Cq_{C}\in\operatorname{int}C and rC>0r_{C}>0 such that the Euclidean ball of radius rCr_{C} centered at qCq_{C} is contained in CC. ⟺AC,b𝖳AC,b⪯Lb,j2Idbfor every C∈𝒞.\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\quad A_{C,b}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{C,b}\preceq L_{b,j}^{2}I_{d_{b}}\quad\text{for every }C\in\mathscr{C}.

All cells of the clipped network vv, including cells outside the training rectangle, occur in this characterization. The proof establishes finiteness and exactness; it makes no claim that constructing the cell collection 𝒞\mathscr{C} is computationally inexpensive. ∎

B.3 Proper covers of constrained classes

For a class 𝒢\mathcal{G} of bounded functions, let 𝒩(ϵ,𝒢,∥⋅∥∞)\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}) be the smallest size of an ϵ\epsilon-cover with centers in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and write H𝒢(ϵ)=log𝒩(ϵ,𝒢,∥⋅∥∞)H_{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon)=\log\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}). These are proper covers: a center must obey all constraints defining the class.

Lemma B.4 (Neural entropy and composition).

Fix a network architecture with PP parameter positions, depth LL, maximum width WW, at most S≤PS\leq P nonzero parameters, parameter magnitudes at most R≥1R\geq 1, bounded projected inputs, and fixed output dimension. Every nonempty subclass obtained by additional functional constraints has a proper cover satisfying

H⁡(ϵ)≤S​log⁡(e​P/S)+S​log​{1+C​R​Cpar/ϵ},log⁡Cpar≤C⁡(L+1)​log​{C⁡(W+1)​R}.H(\epsilon)\leq S\log(eP/S)+S\log\{1+CRC_{\rm par}/\epsilon\},\qquad\log C_{\rm par}\leq C(L+1)\log\{C(W+1)R\}. (B.66)

For the sieves in Equation 2.13, if NN is bounded by a fixed power of nn, then

H𝒱j,N​(n−2)≤C​N​log3⁡(e​n),HℋM​(n−2)≤C​M​log3⁡(e​n),H_{\mathcal{V}_{j,N}}(n^{-2})\leq CN\log^{3}(en),\qquad H_{\mathcal{H}_{M}}(n^{-2})\leq CM\log^{3}(en), (B.67)

with the analogous polynomial-growth condition on the encoder resolution MM. The supremum norm is global because the inputs are projected onto fixed rectangles. For ℱj(N,M)={Fj,v,h:v∈𝒱j,N,h∈ℋM}\mathcal{F}_{j}(N,M)=\{F_{j,v,h}:v\in\mathcal{V}_{j,N},h\in\mathcal{H}_{M}\},

Hℱj​(N,M)​(ϵ)≤H𝒱j,N​(ϵ/2)+HℋM​(ϵ/(2​Lu,j)).H_{\mathcal{F}_{j}(N,M)}(\epsilon)\leq H_{\mathcal{V}_{j,N}}(\epsilon/2)+H_{\mathcal{H}_{M}}(\epsilon/(2L_{u,j})). (B.68)

For any fixed bounded representation hh, including a representation fixed by independent source training,

H{Fj,v,h:v∈𝒱j,N}(ϵ)≤H𝒱j,N(ϵ).H_{\{F_{j,v,h}:v\in\mathcal{V}_{j,N}\}}(\epsilon)\leq H_{\mathcal{V}_{j,N}}(\epsilon). (B.69)
Proof.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be the nonempty function subclass in the first assertion, and write H𝒢(ϵ)=log𝒩(ϵ,𝒢,∥⋅∥∞)H_{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon)=\log\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}), with the proper-cover convention stated immediately before Lemma B.4. Throughout the proof of Equation (B.66), a constant CC may depend on the fixed input dimension DD, output dimension mm, and input rectangle KK, but not on ϵ,P,S,L,W,R\epsilon,P,S,L,W,R or on the particular subclass 𝒢\mathcal{G}. When applying the bound to Equation (2.13), the constant CC may additionally depend on the fixed architecture constants in that equation. If S=0S=0, all trainable parameters are zero, so the nonempty subclass 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains only one realized function and H𝒢​(ϵ)=0H_{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon)=0. The first assertion then holds with the convention 0​log⁡(e​P/0)=00\log(eP/0)=0. We henceforth suppose 1≤S≤P1\leq S\leq P.

Step 1: Network realizations fθf_{\theta} and the global norm. For a vector aa, put |a|max=maxk⁡|ak||a|_{\max}=\max_{k}|a_{k}|; this coordinate maximum norm is distinct from the Euclidean output norm used in ‖f‖∞\|f\|_{\infty}. Let θ∈[−R,R]P\theta\in[-R,R]^{P} list the trainable weights and biases in the fixed network architecture. Let r≤L+1r\leq L+1 be the number of affine maps in its network core, including the affine output map. Under the hidden-layer convention in Section 2.3, r=L+1r=L+1. Write w0=Dw_{0}=D, wr=mw_{r}=m, and wℓ≤Ww_{\ell}\leq W for the hidden-layer widths 1≤ℓ<r1\leq\ell<r. For the weight matrix Aℓθ∈ℝwℓ×wℓ−1A_{\ell}^{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{w_{\ell}\times w_{\ell-1}} and bias bℓθ∈ℝwℓb_{\ell}^{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{w_{\ell}}, define

y0θ​(q)\displaystyle y_{0}^{\theta}(q) =q,\displaystyle=q, (B.70)
yℓθ​(q)\displaystyle y_{\ell}^{\theta}(q) =ρℓ​(Aℓθ​yℓ−1θ​(q)+bℓθ),\displaystyle=\rho_{\ell}\bigl(A_{\ell}^{\theta}y_{\ell-1}^{\theta}(q)+b_{\ell}^{\theta}\bigr), 1≤ℓ≤r,\displaystyle 1\leq\ell\leq r,
fθ​(x)\displaystyle f_{\theta}(x) =Tout​(yrθ​(ΠK​x)).\displaystyle=T_{\rm out}\bigl(y_{r}^{\theta}(\Pi_{K}x)\bigr).

Here ρℓ\rho_{\ell} is coordinatewise ReLU for ℓ<r\ell<r, ρr\rho_{r} is the identity map, ΠK\Pi_{K} is the fixed input projection, and ToutT_{\rm out} is the fixed coordinatewise output clip, or the identity map when no output clip is imposed. Each map ρℓ\rho_{\ell} is 1-Lipschitz in |⋅|max|\cdot|_{\max} and fixes zero; the map ToutT_{\rm out} is 1-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm. Absent connections in the architecture have coefficient zero.

Because ΠK​(ℝD)=K\Pi_{K}(\mathbb{R}^{D})=K and ΠK​q=q\Pi_{K}q=q for q∈Kq\in K, any two parameter vectors θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime} satisfy

‖fθ−fθ′‖∞\displaystyle\|f_{\theta}-f_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{\infty} =supq∈K‖Tout​(yrθ​(q))−Tout​(yrθ′​(q))‖\displaystyle=\sup_{q\in K}\bigl\|T_{\rm out}(y_{r}^{\theta}(q))-T_{\rm out}(y_{r}^{\theta^{\prime}}(q))\bigr\| (B.71)
≤m​supq∈K|yrθ​(q)−yrθ′​(q)|max.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{m}\sup_{q\in K}|y_{r}^{\theta}(q)-y_{r}^{\theta^{\prime}}(q)|_{\max}.

Thus a uniform bound on the fixed rectangle KK in Equation (B.71) controls the global supremum norm, not merely a norm on observed inputs.

Step 2: A parameter-to-function bound CparC_{\rm par}. Define the fixed input bound B0B_{0}, augmented width w∗w_{*}, and layer factor Q∗Q_{*} by

B0=max⁡{1,supq∈K|q|max},w∗=max⁡{D,m,W,1},Q∗=(w∗+1)​R.B_{0}=\max\{1,\sup_{q\in K}|q|_{\max}\},\qquad w_{*}=\max\{D,m,W,1\},\qquad Q_{*}=(w_{*}+1)R. (B.72)

Since every entry of Aℓθ,bℓθA_{\ell}^{\theta},b_{\ell}^{\theta} has magnitude at most RR, Equation (B.70) gives M0≤B0M_{0}\leq B_{0} and

Mℓ\displaystyle M_{\ell} ≤w∗​R​Mℓ−1+R\displaystyle\leq w_{*}RM_{\ell-1}+R (B.73)
≤w∗RB0Q∗ℓ−1+R≤(w∗+1)RB0Q∗ℓ−1=B0Q∗ℓ,1≤ℓ≤r.\displaystyle\leq w_{*}RB_{0}Q_{*}^{\ell-1}+R\leq(w_{*}+1)RB_{0}Q_{*}^{\ell-1}=B_{0}Q_{*}^{\ell},\qquad 1\leq\ell\leq r.

The second line is an induction on ℓ\ell; its last inequality uses B0​Q∗ℓ−1≥1B_{0}Q_{*}^{\ell-1}\geq 1.

Now fix θ,θ′∈[−R,R]P\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in[-R,R]^{P}, and define their parameter distance and activation differences by

dθ=|θ−θ′|max,Eℓ=supq∈K|yℓθ​(q)−yℓθ′​(q)|max,E0=0.d_{\theta}=|\theta-\theta^{\prime}|_{\max},\qquad E_{\ell}=\sup_{q\in K}|y_{\ell}^{\theta}(q)-y_{\ell}^{\theta^{\prime}}(q)|_{\max},\qquad E_{0}=0. (B.74)

For each input q∈Kq\in K, the difference of the two affine preactivations in layer ℓ\ell is exactly

Aℓθ​yℓ−1θ​(q)+bℓθ−Aℓθ′​yℓ−1θ′​(q)−bℓθ′\displaystyle A_{\ell}^{\theta}y_{\ell-1}^{\theta}(q)+b_{\ell}^{\theta}-A_{\ell}^{\theta^{\prime}}y_{\ell-1}^{\theta^{\prime}}(q)-b_{\ell}^{\theta^{\prime}} (B.75)
=Aℓθ​{yℓ−1θ​(q)−yℓ−1θ′​(q)}+(Aℓθ−Aℓθ′)​yℓ−1θ′​(q)+(bℓθ−bℓθ′).\displaystyle=A_{\ell}^{\theta}\{y_{\ell-1}^{\theta}(q)-y_{\ell-1}^{\theta^{\prime}}(q)\}+(A_{\ell}^{\theta}-A_{\ell}^{\theta^{\prime}})y_{\ell-1}^{\theta^{\prime}}(q)+(b_{\ell}^{\theta}-b_{\ell}^{\theta^{\prime}}).

Using the 1-Lipschitz property of ρℓ\rho_{\ell}, the row length bound wℓ−1≤w∗w_{\ell-1}\leq w_{*}, and the entrywise difference bound dθd_{\theta} in Equation (B.75) yields

Eℓ\displaystyle E_{\ell} ≤w∗​R​Eℓ−1+w∗​dθ​Mℓ−1+dθ\displaystyle\leq w_{*}RE_{\ell-1}+w_{*}d_{\theta}M_{\ell-1}+d_{\theta} (B.76)
≤Q∗​Eℓ−1+(w∗+1)​B0​Q∗ℓ−1​dθ.\displaystyle\leq Q_{*}E_{\ell-1}+(w_{*}+1)B_{0}Q_{*}^{\ell-1}d_{\theta}.

The second inequality follows from Equations (B.72) and (B.73). Iterating Equation (B.76) from E0=0E_{0}=0 gives the explicit finite sum

Eℓ\displaystyle E_{\ell} ≤(w∗+1)​B0​dθ​∑k=1ℓQ∗ℓ−k​Q∗k−1\displaystyle\leq(w_{*}+1)B_{0}d_{\theta}\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}Q_{*}^{\ell-k}Q_{*}^{k-1} (B.77)
=ℓ(w∗+1)B0Q∗ℓ−1dθ≤ℓB0Q∗ℓdθ,1≤ℓ≤r.\displaystyle=\ell(w_{*}+1)B_{0}Q_{*}^{\ell-1}d_{\theta}\leq\ell B_{0}Q_{*}^{\ell}d_{\theta},\qquad 1\leq\ell\leq r.

The last inequality uses w∗+1≤Q∗w_{*}+1\leq Q_{*}, which follows from R≥1R\geq 1. Combining Equations (B.71) and (B.77), and using r≤L+1r\leq L+1, proves

‖fθ−fθ′‖∞≤Cpar​|θ−θ′|max,Cpar=m​B0​(L+1)​Q∗L+1.\|f_{\theta}-f_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\rm par}|\theta-\theta^{\prime}|_{\max},\qquad C_{\rm par}=\sqrt{m}\,B_{0}(L+1)Q_{*}^{L+1}. (B.78)

This comparison holds for all pairs θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime} in the parameter box, hence in particular for pairs with a common support. Since w∗+1≤C⁡(W+1)w_{*}+1\leq C(W+1), with D,mD,m fixed, the constant CparC_{\rm par} in Equation (B.78) satisfies

log⁡Cpar\displaystyle\log C_{\rm par} =12​log⁡m+log⁡B0+log⁡(L+1)+(L+1)​log​Q∗\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\log m+\log B_{0}+\log(L+1)+(L+1)\log Q_{*} (B.79)
≤C⁡(L+1)​log⁡{C⁡(W+1)​R}.\displaystyle\leq C(L+1)\log\{C(W+1)R\}.

Here log⁡(L+1)≤L+1\log(L+1)\leq L+1, and the remaining fixed terms are absorbed by increasing CC. This proves the second inequality in Equation (B.66).

Step 3: Supports JJ, parameter cells BB, and proper centers. Define the sparse parameter set ΘS\Theta_{S}, the feasible parameter set Θ𝒢\Theta_{\mathcal{G}}, and the coordinate boxes ΘJ\Theta_{J} by

ΘS\displaystyle\Theta_{S} ={θ∈[−R,R]P:|supp⁡(θ)|≤S},\displaystyle=\{\theta\in[-R,R]^{P}:|\operatorname{supp}(\theta)|\leq S\}, (B.80)
Θ𝒢\displaystyle\Theta_{\mathcal{G}} ={θ∈ΘS:fθ∈𝒢},\displaystyle=\{\theta\in\Theta_{S}:f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{G}\},
𝒥S\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{S} ={J⊆{1,…,P}:|J|=S},\displaystyle=\{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,P\}:|J|=S\},
ΘJ\displaystyle\Theta_{J} ={θ∈[−R,R]P:θk=0 for k∉J},J∈𝒥S.\displaystyle=\{\theta\in[-R,R]^{P}:\theta_{k}=0\text{ for }k\notin J\},\qquad J\in\mathcal{J}_{S}.

Every support supp⁡(θ)\operatorname{supp}(\theta) with at most SS elements is contained in some set J∈𝒥SJ\in\mathcal{J}_{S}. Consequently, ΘS=⋃J∈𝒥SΘJ\Theta_{S}=\bigcup_{J\in\mathcal{J}_{S}}\Theta_{J}. Coordinates in JJ are allowed to equal zero; thus this union includes all supports of size less than SS without separately counting their sizes. Moreover,

|𝒥S|=(PS)≤PSS!≤(e​PS)S.|\mathcal{J}_{S}|=\binom{P}{S}\leq\frac{P^{S}}{S!}\leq\left(\frac{eP}{S}\right)^{S}. (B.81)

For the last inequality, the exponential series gives eS≥SS/S!e^{S}\geq S^{S}/S!, or equivalently S!≥(S/e)SS!\geq(S/e)^{S}.

Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and put δ=ϵ/(2​Cpar)\delta=\epsilon/(2C_{\rm par}). Partition each active coordinate interval [−R,R][-R,R] into kδ=max⁡{1,⌈2​R/δ⌉}k_{\delta}=\max\{1,\lceil 2R/\delta\rceil\} intervals of length at most δ\delta, assigning shared endpoints to one interval. Then each box ΘJ\Theta_{J} is partitioned into at most kδSk_{\delta}^{S} parameter cells BB, each of coordinate maximum diameter at most δ\delta. For every pair (J,B)(J,B) for which B∩Θ𝒢≠∅B\cap\Theta_{\mathcal{G}}\neq\varnothing, choose one parameter vector θJ,B∈B∩Θ𝒢\theta^{J,B}\in B\cap\Theta_{\mathcal{G}}. The finite set

𝒞ϵ={fθJ,B:J∈𝒥S,B∩Θ𝒢≠∅}⊆𝒢\mathcal{C}_{\epsilon}=\{f_{\theta^{J,B}}:J\in\mathcal{J}_{S},\ B\cap\Theta_{\mathcal{G}}\neq\varnothing\}\subseteq\mathcal{G} (B.82)

is a proper cover. Indeed, for any f∈𝒢f\in\mathcal{G}, take a feasible parameterization f=fθf=f_{\theta}, select J∈𝒥SJ\in\mathcal{J}_{S} with supp⁡(θ)⊆J\operatorname{supp}(\theta)\subseteq J, and let BB be its parameter cell. Equation (B.78) then gives

‖f−fθJ,B‖∞≤Cpar​|θ−θJ,B|max≤Cpar​δ=ϵ/2≤ϵ.\|f-f_{\theta^{J,B}}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\rm par}|\theta-\theta^{J,B}|_{\max}\leq C_{\rm par}\delta=\epsilon/2\leq\epsilon. (B.83)

No closedness of Θ𝒢\Theta_{\mathcal{G}} is required: only one point from each of finitely many nonempty intersections is chosen. In particular, the center fθJ,Bf_{\theta^{J,B}} satisfies every functional constraint defining 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The partition of the parameter box is not a rounding rule for θ\theta; a corner of its cell need not satisfy those constraints.

The interval count satisfies kδ≤1+2​R/δ=1+4​R​Cpar/ϵk_{\delta}\leq 1+2R/\delta=1+4RC_{\rm par}/\epsilon. Equations (B.81)–(B.83) therefore imply

𝒩(ϵ,𝒢,∥⋅∥∞)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}) ≤|𝒞ϵ|≤(PS)​kδS\displaystyle\leq|\mathcal{C}_{\epsilon}|\leq\binom{P}{S}\,k_{\delta}^{S} (B.84)
≤(e​PS)S​(1+4​R​Cparϵ)S.\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{eP}{S}\right)^{S}\left(1+\frac{4RC_{\rm par}}{\epsilon}\right)^{S}.

Taking logarithms in Equation (B.84) proves the first inequality in Equation (B.66). Different parameter cells or support boxes may represent the same function; such duplications only decrease the required cover size.

Step 4: The sieve bound C​N​log3​(e​n)CN\log^{3}(en). First consider a core sieve 𝒩D,m​(N)\mathcal{N}_{D,m}(N) with fixed D,mD,m. PN\displaystyle P_{N} =WN​(D+1)+(LN−1)​WN​(WN+1)+m⁡(WN+1)\displaystyle=W_{N}(D+1)+(L_{N}-1)W_{N}(W_{N}+1)+m(W_{N}+1) (B.85)
≤C⁡(LN+1)​(WN+1)2≤C​N2​log⁡(e​N),\displaystyle\leq C(L_{N}+1)(W_{N}+1)^{2}\leq CN^{2}\log(eN),

Let 𝒢N\mathcal{G}_{N} be any nonempty constrained subclass of this projected, possibly output-clipped sieve. Fix cϵ>0c_{\epsilon}>0, independent of n,Nn,N, and take ϵ=cϵ​n−2\epsilon=c_{\epsilon}n^{-2} with n≥2n\geq 2. Since RN​Cpar,N​n2≥1R_{N}C_{{\rm par},N}n^{2}\geq 1,

For the head sieve 𝒱j,N\mathcal{V}_{j,N}, set D=DjD=D_{j}, m=djm=d_{j}, K=𝒦jK=\mathcal{K}_{j}, and Tout=clipbjT_{\rm out}=\operatorname{clip}_{b_{j}}. H𝒱j,N​(cϵ​n−2)≤C​N​log3⁡(e​n),HℋM​(cϵ​n−2)≤C​M​log3⁡(e​n).H_{\mathcal{V}_{j,N}}(c_{\epsilon}n^{-2})\leq CN\log^{3}(en),\qquad H_{\mathcal{H}_{M}}(c_{\epsilon}n^{-2})\leq CM\log^{3}(en). (B.90)

Step 5: A proper product cover for ℱj​(N,M)\mathcal{F}_{j}(N,M). Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0. The constant Lu,jL_{u,j} is strictly positive by the convention following Equation (2.15). Choose proper covers {v(a):1≤a≤KV}⊆𝒱j,N\{v^{(a)}:1\leq a\leq K_{V}\}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{j,N} and {h(b):1≤b≤KH}⊆ℋM\{h^{(b)}:1\leq b\leq K_{H}\}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{M}, where

KV\displaystyle K_{V} =𝒩(ϵ/2,𝒱j,N,∥⋅∥∞),\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\epsilon/2,\mathcal{V}_{j,N},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}), (B.91)
KH\displaystyle K_{H} =𝒩(ϵ/(2Lu,j),ℋM,∥⋅∥∞).\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\epsilon/(2L_{u,j}),\mathcal{H}_{M},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}).

For any pair (v,h)∈𝒱j,N×ℋM(v,h)\in\mathcal{V}_{j,N}\times\mathcal{H}_{M}, select indices a,ba,b with ‖v−v(a)‖∞≤ϵ/2\|v-v^{(a)}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon/2 and ‖h−h(b)‖∞≤ϵ/(2​Lu,j)\|h-h^{(b)}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon/(2L_{u,j}). ={v⁡(x,h⁡(z0),zc,τ)−v(a)​(x,h⁡(z0),zc,τ)}\displaystyle=\{v(x,h(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau)-v^{(a)}(x,h(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau)\}
+{v(a)​(x,h⁡(z0),zc,τ)−v(a)​(x,h(b)​(z0),zc,τ)}.\displaystyle+\{v^{(a)}(x,h(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau)-v^{(a)}(x,h^{(b)}(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau)\}.

Taking the supremum over the field inputs in Equation (B.92) gives

‖Fj,v,h−Fj,v(a),h(b)‖∞\displaystyle\|F_{j,v,h}-F_{j,v^{(a)},h^{(b)}}\|_{\infty} ≤‖v−v(a)‖∞+Lu,j​‖h−h(b)‖∞\displaystyle\leq\|v-v^{(a)}\|_{\infty}+L_{u,j}\|h-h^{(b)}\|_{\infty} (B.93)
≤ϵ/2+Lu,j​ϵ/(2​Lu,j)=ϵ.\displaystyle\leq\epsilon/2+L_{u,j}\epsilon/(2L_{u,j})=\epsilon.

Every composed center Fj,v(a),h(b)F_{j,v^{(a)},h^{(b)}} belongs to ℱj​(N,M)\mathcal{F}_{j}(N,M). Thus these centers form a proper cover of size at most KV​KHK_{V}K_{H}, and

Hℱj​(N,M)​(ϵ)\displaystyle H_{\mathcal{F}_{j}(N,M)}(\epsilon) ≤log⁡(KV​KH)=log⁡KV+log⁡KH\displaystyle\leq\log(K_{V}K_{H})=\log K_{V}+\log K_{H} (B.94)
=H𝒱j,N​(ϵ/2)+HℋM​(ϵ/(2​Lu,j)).\displaystyle=H_{\mathcal{V}_{j,N}}(\epsilon/2)+H_{\mathcal{H}_{M}}(\epsilon/(2L_{u,j})).

This is Equation (B.68). The Lipschitz bound used here is the representation-input bound of the head v(a)v^{(a)}; no Lipschitz bound on the fitted representation hh is required.

Step 6: Frozen representations hh and source conditioning. Fix a bounded representation hh, and put ℱh={Fj,v,h:v∈𝒱j,N}\mathcal{F}_{h}=\{F_{j,v,h}:v\in\mathcal{V}_{j,N}\}. For any two heads v,v′∈𝒱j,Nv,v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}_{j,N}, their representation argument is identical, so Equation (2.4) yields

‖Fj,v,h−Fj,v′,h‖∞\displaystyle\|F_{j,v,h}-F_{j,v^{\prime},h}\|_{\infty} =supx,z,τ‖v⁡(x,h⁡(z0),zc,τ)−v′​(x,h⁡(z0),zc,τ)‖\displaystyle=\sup_{x,z,\tau}\|v(x,h(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau)-v^{\prime}(x,h(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau)\| (B.95)
≤‖v−v′‖∞.\displaystyle\leq\|v-v^{\prime}\|_{\infty}.

Consequently, the images of any proper ϵ\epsilon-cover of 𝒱j,N\mathcal{V}_{j,N} under the map v↦Fj,v,hv\mapsto F_{j,v,h} form a proper ϵ\epsilon-cover of ℱh\mathcal{F}_{h}. In particular,

𝒩(ϵ,ℱh,∥⋅∥∞)≤𝒩(ϵ,𝒱j,N,∥⋅∥∞).\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{F}_{h},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})\leq\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{V}_{j,N},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}). (B.96)

Taking logarithms in Equation (B.96) proves Equation (B.69). The bound contains no cover of hh, and hence no dependence on the number or values of parameters used to realize hh.

For the source-trained case, take j=tj=t and let 𝒮\mathscr{S} be the source-and-anchor sigma-field defined in Section 3.3. The fitted representation h^s\widehat{h}_{s} is 𝒮\mathscr{S}-measurable, and 𝒮\mathscr{S} is independent of the target training sample. Choose a deterministic proper head cover {v(a):1≤a≤Kϵ}\{v^{(a)}:1\leq a\leq K_{\epsilon}\}, where Kϵ=𝒩(ϵ,𝒱t,N,∥⋅∥∞)K_{\epsilon}=\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{V}_{t,N},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}). For each realization ω\omega of the source information, the explicit center set

𝒞ϵ​(ω)={Ft,v(a),h^s​(ω):1≤a≤Kϵ}\mathcal{C}_{\epsilon}(\omega)=\{F_{t,v^{(a)},\widehat{h}_{s}(\omega)}:1\leq a\leq K_{\epsilon}\} (B.97)

is a proper ϵ\epsilon-cover of ℱh^s​(ω)\mathcal{F}_{\widehat{h}_{s}(\omega)}, by Equation (B.95). These centers are 𝒮\mathscr{S}-measurable at every field input because the head centers v(a)v^{(a)} are deterministic continuous functions and h^s\widehat{h}_{s} has the measurable version stipulated in Section 2. Therefore no additional measurable selection of a source-dependent parameter cover is needed. The bound Hℱh^s​(ω)​(ϵ)≤H𝒱t,N​(ϵ)H_{\mathcal{F}_{\widehat{h}_{s}(\omega)}}(\epsilon)\leq H_{\mathcal{V}_{t,N}}(\epsilon) holds for every admissible realization ω\omega, with the same constant. Independence from target training is not needed for the deterministic inequality (B.95); it ensures that conditioning on 𝒮\mathscr{S} fixes this cover without changing the target sampling law when the cover is subsequently used in Lemma C.1. ∎

Appendix C Regression bounds and main theorem proofs

C.1 A bounded relative-deviation inequality

Lemma C.1 (Relative deviations, least squares, and auxiliary clusters).

Let (Wi,Ui)(W_{i},U_{i}), 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, be independent observations with common law, ‖Ui‖≤BU\|U_{i}\|\leq B_{U}, and let f0​(W)=𝔼​(U∣W)f_{0}(W)=\mathbb{E}(U\mid W). Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a nonempty class of predictors bounded by BVB_{V}, fixed independently of these observations. Set K=BU+BVK=B_{U}+B_{V}, K0=1+BU+BVK_{0}=1+B_{U}+B_{V}, s⁡(f)=‖f−f0‖L2​(PW)2s(f)=\|f-f_{0}\|_{L_{2}(P_{W})}^{2}, and Df=ℓf−ℓf0D_{f}=\ell_{f}-\ell_{f_{0}}. For every x≥0x\geq 0, with probability at least 1−e−x1-e^{-x}, simultaneously for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F},

|(Pn−P)​Df|≤14​s​(f)+bn​(x),bn​(x)=C​K02​Hℱ​(n−2)+x+1n.|(P_{n}-P)D_{f}|\leq\tfrac{1}{4}s(f)+b_{n}(x),\qquad b_{n}(x)=CK_{0}^{2}\frac{H_{\mathcal{F}}(n^{-2})+x+1}{n}. (C.1)

Consequently any measurable ϵ\epsilon-minimizer of Pn​ℓfP_{n}\ell_{f} over ℱ\mathcal{F} satisfies, on the same event,

s⁡(f^)≤53​inff∈ℱs⁡(f)+83​bn​(x)+43​ϵ.s(\widehat{f})\leq\tfrac{5}{3}\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}}s(f)+\tfrac{8}{3}b_{n}(x)+\tfrac{4}{3}\epsilon. (C.2)

In expectation the same inequality holds with bn​(x)b_{n}(x) replaced by C​K02​{Hℱ​(n−2)+1}/nCK_{0}^{2}\{H_{\mathcal{F}}(n^{-2})+1\}/n. The results hold conditionally on independent information fixing the class. They also hold when each original observation has a fixed number of conditionally independent auxiliary draws and its loss is their average, or when the loss is integrated over the auxiliary draws exactly. In these cases nn counts original observations.

P​Df2\displaystyle PD_{f}^{2} ≤25​K2​𝔼​‖af​(W)‖2=25​K2​s​(f).\displaystyle\leq 25K^{2}\mathbb{E}\|a_{f}(W)\|^{2}=25K^{2}s(f). (C.7)

In particular, the centered variable Yi,f=Df​(Oi)−P​DfY_{i,f}=D_{f}(O_{i})-PD_{f} satisfies

Step 2: A scalar concentration calculation for a fixed predictor ff.

Let YY be any centered real random variable satisfying |Y|≤b|Y|\leq b and 𝔼​Y2≤σ2\mathbb{E}Y^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}. For k≥2k\geq 2, |𝔼​Yk|≤bk−2​σ2|\mathbb{E}Y^{k}|\leq b^{k-2}\sigma^{2}. The factorial inequality k!≥2⋅3k−2k!\geq 2\cdot 3^{k-2} follows by induction from its equality at k=2k=2. Consequently, for |t|​b<3|t|b<3, the absolutely convergent exponential series yields

≤exp⁡{t2​σ22​(1−|t|​b/3)}.\displaystyle\leq\exp\left\{\frac{t^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2(1-|t|b/3)}\right\}. (C.9)

To make the exponential-tail calculation explicit, put V=n​σ2V=n\sigma^{2}, c=b/3c=b/3, and, for V>0V>0 and u>0u>0, α=2​u/V\alpha=\sqrt{2u/V} and t=α/(1+c​α)t=\alpha/(1+c\alpha). Markov’s inequality then gives

=exp⁡{−2​u+c​α​u1+c​α+u1+c​α}=e−u.\displaystyle=\exp\left\{-\frac{2u+c\alpha u}{1+c\alpha}+\frac{u}{1+c\alpha}\right\}=e^{-u}.

Use Equation C.8 in Equation C.10, with b=10​K2b=10K^{2} and σ2=25​K2​s​(f)\sigma^{2}=25K^{2}s(f). The elementary inequality A​B≤A2/4+B2AB\leq A^{2}/4+B^{2}, applied with A=s⁡(f)A=\sqrt{s(f)} and B=50​K2​u/nB=\sqrt{50K^{2}u/n}, gives

Step 5: Conditioning on independent information and averaging auxiliary draws.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a sigma-field independent of the observations O1,…,OnO_{1},\ldots,O_{n}, and suppose that ℬ\mathcal{B} fixes the predictor class ℱ\mathcal{F}. Conditional on almost every realization of ℬ\mathcal{B}, the observations retain their product law, the mean f0f_{0} is unchanged, and the preceding proof applies to the now fixed class ℱ\mathcal{F}. In particular, Equation C.15 can be integrated conditionally on ℬ\mathcal{B}. This establishes both conditional assertions.

For the cluster assertion, let ViV_{i} denote original observation ii, and let Oi,kO_{i,k}, 1≤k≤m1\leq k\leq m, be its regression observations obtained from the mm auxiliary draws. Each Oi,kO_{i,k} has the same marginal law as OO; the vectors (Vi,Oi,1,…,Oi,m)(V_{i},O_{i,1},\ldots,O_{i,m}) are independent over ii. Define the cluster excess loss D¯f,i=m−1​∑k=1mDf​(Oi,k)\overline{D}_{f,i}=m^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{m}D_{f}(O_{i,k}). Equations (C.5)–(C.7) and the inequality (m−1​∑kdk)2≤m−1​∑kdk2(m^{-1}\sum_{k}d_{k})^{2}\leq m^{-1}\sum_{k}d_{k}^{2} give

𝔼​D¯f,i=s⁡(f),|D¯f,i|≤5​K2,𝔼​D¯f,i 2≤1m​∑k=1m𝔼​Df​(Oi,k)2≤25​K2​s​(f).\mathbb{E}\overline{D}_{f,i}=s(f),\qquad|\overline{D}_{f,i}|\leq 5K^{2},\qquad\mathbb{E}\overline{D}_{f,i}^{\,2}\leq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}D_{f}(O_{i,k})^{2}\leq 25K^{2}s(f). (C.16)

The exact auxiliary-integrated excess loss is Df,iint=𝔼⁡{Df​(Oi,1)∣Vi}D_{f,i}^{\rm int}=\mathbb{E}\{D_{f}(O_{i,1})\mid V_{i}\}. The tower property and conditional Jensen’s inequality give the same three bounds in Equation C.16 for Df,iintD_{f,i}^{\rm int}. The loss differences for either cluster average also retain the bound 2​K​δn2K\delta_{n} in Equation C.13, by averaging or conditional expectation. Thus all concentration, covering, and minimization steps apply to the nn independent cluster losses. None of these steps treats the n​mnm auxiliary regression observations as independent; the denominator in Equation C.1 remains nn. ∎

C.2 Joint neural learning and the frozen comparator

Lemma C.2 (Joint neural regression and source deficiency).

For task jj, suppose its bounded-regression part of Assumption 1 and its part of Assumption 2 hold. Let (v^j,h^j)(\widehat{v}_{j},\widehat{h}_{j}) be an ϵj\epsilon_{j}-minimizer of the empirical loss over 𝒱j,N×ℋM\mathcal{V}_{j,N}\times\mathcal{H}_{M}, with N,MN,M at most polynomial in njn_{j} and above the fixed approximation threshold. Then

𝔼ℰj(Fj,v^j,h^j)≤C{ζj2+N−2rj/Dj+M−2βj/p+(N+M)​log3⁡(e​nj)nj+ϵj}.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{j}(F_{j,\widehat{v}_{j},\widehat{h}_{j}})\leq C\left\{\zeta_{j}^{2}+N^{-2r_{j}/D_{j}}+M^{-2\beta_{j}/p}+\frac{(N+M)\log^{3}(en_{j})}{n_{j}}+\epsilon_{j}\right\}. (C.17)

Also 𝔼​𝒟j​(h^j)\mathbb{E}\mathcal{D}_{j}(\widehat{h}_{j}) is at most the left side of Equation C.17.

Fix the task index j∈{s,t}j\in\{s,t\}, and let ℱj(N,M)={Fj,v,h:v∈𝒱j,N,h∈ℋM}\mathcal{F}_{j}(N,M)=\{F_{j,v,h}:v\in\mathcal{V}_{j,N},\ h\in\mathcal{H}_{M}\} be the joint field class in Lemma B.4. Its population norm is ∥⋅∥j=∥⋅∥L2​(νj)\|\cdot\|_{j}=\|\cdot\|_{L_{2}(\nu_{j})}, and its regression mean is vj0v_{j}^{0} from Equation 2.3.

Apply Lemma B.2 to the functions hj,0h_{j,0} and gj,0g_{j,0} in Assumption 2. There are comparators hM∈ℋMh_{M}\in\mathcal{H}_{M} and vj,N∈𝒱j,Nv_{j,N}\in\mathcal{V}_{j,N} satisfying

∥hM−hj,0∥∞≤CM−βj/p,∥vj,N−gj,0∥∞,𝒦j≤CN−rj/Dj.\|h_{M}-h_{j,0}\|_{\infty}\leq CM^{-\beta_{j}/p},\qquad\|v_{j,N}-g_{j,0}\|_{\infty,\mathcal{K}_{j}}\leq CN^{-r_{j}/D_{j}}. (C.18)

Here feasibility of the head vj,Nv_{j,N}, not merely its value approximation, follows from Equations B.3 and 3.2. Indeed, with ηmin,j=minb∈{x,u,τ}⁡ηb,j>0\eta_{\min,j}=\min_{b\in\{x,u,\tau\}}\eta_{b,j}>0, the approximation threshold can be chosen so that CN−(rj−1)/Dj≤ηmin,jCN^{-(r_{j}-1)/D_{j}}\leq\eta_{\min,j}. For the encoder hMh_{M}, the value approximation in Equation C.18 suffices; no encoder derivative bound is needed.

Step 2: Bound the comparator’s population excess risk.

qM​(w)=(x,hM​(z0),zc,τ),q0​(w)=(x,hj,0​(z0),zc,τ).q_{M}(w)=(x,h_{M}(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau),\qquad q_{0}(w)=(x,h_{j,0}(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau).

e3​(w)\displaystyle e_{3}(w) =gj,0​(q0​(w))−vj0​(w).\displaystyle=g_{j,0}(q_{0}(w))-v_{j}^{0}(w). (C.19)

By Equations 2.4 and C.19, Fj,vj,N,hM−vj0=e1+e2+e3F_{j,v_{j,N},h_{M}}-v_{j}^{0}=e_{1}+e_{2}+e_{3}. Equation (C.18), the representation-block bound Lipu⁡(gj,0;𝒦j)≤Lu,j\operatorname{Lip}_{u}(g_{j,0};\mathcal{K}_{j})\leq L_{u,j} in Equation 3.2, and Equation 3.1 yield

≤C{ζj2+N−2rj/Dj+M−2βj/p}.\displaystyle\leq C\{\zeta_{j}^{2}+N^{-2r_{j}/D_{j}}+M^{-2\beta_{j}/p}\}. (C.21)

Step 3: Count both fitted networks and apply the regression oracle.

The proper composition cover in Equation B.68 gives

Hℱj​(N,M)​(nj−2)\displaystyle H_{\mathcal{F}_{j}(N,M)}(n_{j}^{-2}) ≤H𝒱j,N​(nj−2/2)+HℋM​(nj−2/(2​Lu,j))\displaystyle\leq H_{\mathcal{V}_{j,N}}(n_{j}^{-2}/2)+H_{\mathcal{H}_{M}}(n_{j}^{-2}/(2L_{u,j}))
≤C⁡(N+M)​log3⁡(e​nj).\displaystyle\leq C(N+M)\log^{3}(en_{j}). (C.22)

The last inequality uses Equations B.66 and B.67, the fixed positive constant Lu,jL_{u,j}, and the assumed polynomial-growth bounds on N,MN,M. Lemma C.3 (Expected profile at the source representation).

Under the target bounded-label condition and Assumption 3, for all sufficiently large NN,

Moreover, Ka,D​(n)≤2​nθK_{a,D}(n)\leq 2n^{\theta} for sufficiently large nn, so these resolutions satisfy the polynomial-growth requirements in Lemmas B.4 and C.2. They also eventually exceed every fixed approximation threshold required by Lemma B.2.

≤C{ζs2+Ns−2rs/Ds+Ms−2βs/p+Ns​ℓns3ns+Ms​ℓns3ns+ns−2}.\displaystyle\leq C\left\{\zeta_{s}^{2}+N_{s}^{-2r_{s}/D_{s}}+M_{s}^{-2\beta_{s}/p}+\frac{N_{s}\ell_{n_{s}}^{3}}{n_{s}}+\frac{M_{s}\ell_{n_{s}}^{3}}{n_{s}}+n_{s}^{-2}\right\}. (C.30)

(C.33)

Using Equation 3.9 and Equation C.29 with (a,D,n)=(rt,Dt,nt)(a,D,n)=(r_{t},D_{t},n_{t}), the right side of Equation C.33 is at most

C.4 Neural residual approximation and conditional complexity

Lemma C.4 (Residual comparators and conditional neural entropy).

Condition on 𝒮\mathscr{S}. For the class in Equation 3.14, let ℱA(N,M)={Ft,v,hh^s,a:v∈𝒱t,N,a∈ℛA,M}\mathcal{F}_{A}(N,M)=\{F_{t,v,h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a}}:v\in\mathcal{V}_{t,N},\ a\in\mathcal{R}_{A,M}\}. For N,MN,M bounded by fixed powers of nn,

Qt,N(h^s)≤C{κA𝒟s(h^s)+ζA2+N−2rt/Dt+Lu,t2δA2}on Es,A.Q_{t,N}(\widehat{h}_{s})\leq C\{\kappa_{A}\mathcal{D}_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s})+\zeta_{A}^{2}+N^{-2r_{t}/D_{t}}+L_{u,t}^{2}\delta_{A}^{2}\}\quad\hbox{on }E_{s,A}. (C.39)

Fix a realization of the target-independent sigma-field 𝒮\mathscr{S}. In this conditional argument the fitted source representation h^s\widehat{h}_{s} is a fixed function taking values in [−1,1]dh[-1,1]^{d_{h}}, and the residual class ℛA,M\mathcal{R}_{A,M} is specified by Equation 3.13.

Step 1: Compare two residual encoders with the same source branch h^s\widehat{h}_{s}.

Coordinatewise clipping to a rectangle is Euclidean nonexpansive. Thus, for any a,a′∈ℛA,Ma,a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{A,M} and z0∈𝒵0z_{0}\in\mathcal{Z}_{0},

‖hh^s,a​(z0)−hh^s,a′​(z0)‖\displaystyle\|h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a}(z_{0})-h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a^{\prime}}(z_{0})\|
=‖clip1⁡{h^s​(z0)+a⁡(z0,IA)}−clip1⁡{h^s​(z0)+a′​(z0,IA)}‖\displaystyle\quad=\big\|\operatorname{clip}_{1}\{\widehat{h}_{s}(z_{0})+a(z_{0,I_{A}})\}-\operatorname{clip}_{1}\{\widehat{h}_{s}(z_{0})+a^{\prime}(z_{0,I_{A}})\}\big\|
≤‖a⁡(z0,IA)−a′​(z0,IA)‖.\displaystyle\quad\leq\|a(z_{0,I_{A}})-a^{\prime}(z_{0,I_{A}})\|.

For v,v′∈𝒱t,Nv,v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}_{t,N}, add and subtract Ft,v′,hh^s,aF_{t,v^{\prime},h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a}}. The representation-block constraint Lipu⁡(v′)≤Lu,t\operatorname{Lip}_{u}(v^{\prime})\leq L_{u,t} from Equation 2.15 then gives
