≤‖Ft,v,hh^s,a−Ft,v′,hh^s,a‖∞+‖Ft,v′,hh^s,a−Ft,v′,hh^s,a′‖∞\displaystyle\quad\leq\|F_{t,v,h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a}}-F_{t,v^{\prime},h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a}}\|_{\infty}+\|F_{t,v^{\prime},h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a}}-F_{t,v^{\prime},h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a^{\prime}}}\|_{\infty}
≤‖v−v′‖∞+Lu,t​‖hh^s,a−hh^s,a′‖∞≤‖v−v′‖∞+Lu,t​‖a−a′‖∞.\displaystyle\quad\leq\|v-v^{\prime}\|_{\infty}+L_{u,t}\|h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a}-h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a^{\prime}}\|_{\infty}\leq\|v-v^{\prime}\|_{\infty}+L_{u,t}\|a-a^{\prime}\|_{\infty}. (C.41)

C.5 A penalized oracle with joint-class entropy

Lemma C.5 (Conditional penalized least-squares oracle).

Condition on target-independent information fixing a class of pairs 𝒫={(v,h)}\mathcal{P}=\{(v,h)\}, its composed field class ℱ\mathcal{F}, and a nonnegative functional penalty As​(h)A_{s}(h). Suppose the bounded-regression conditions of Lemma C.1 hold. Write n=ntn=n_{t}, ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, and bℱ​(x)=C​(1+Kt)2​{Hℱ​(n−2)+x+1}/nb_{\mathcal{F}}(x)=C(1+K_{t})^{2}\{H_{\mathcal{F}}(n^{-2})+x+1\}/n. On an event of conditional probability at least 1−e−x1-e^{-x}, every ϵ\epsilon-minimizer (v^λ,h^λ)(\widehat{v}_{\lambda},\widehat{h}_{\lambda}) of the empirical squared loss plus λ​As​(h)\lambda A_{s}(h), with λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, satisfies

ℰt​(F^λ)+4​λ3​As​(h^λ)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})+\tfrac{4\lambda}{3}A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda})
≤inf(v,h)∈𝒫{53​ℰt​(Ft,v,h)+4​λ3​As​(h)}+83​bℱ​(x)+43​ϵ.\displaystyle\quad\leq\inf_{(v,h)\in\mathcal{P}}\left\{\tfrac{5}{3}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h})+\tfrac{4\lambda}{3}A_{s}(h)\right\}+\tfrac{8}{3}b_{\mathcal{F}}(x)+\tfrac{4}{3}\epsilon. (C.48)

The event is simultaneous in λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 for the fixed class. At λ=0\lambda=0, the penalty term is omitted throughout. For a fixed λ\lambda, the conditional expectation version replaces bℱ​(x)b_{\mathcal{F}}(x) by C​(1+Kt)2​{Hℱ​(n−2)+1}/nC(1+K_{t})^{2}\{H_{\mathcal{F}}(n^{-2})+1\}/n.

Proof.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the target-independent sigma-field fixing the pair class 𝒫\mathcal{P}, its composed field class ℱ\mathcal{F}, and the functional penalty AsA_{s}. We work conditional on a realization of ℬ\mathcal{B}. In particular, the population operator PP is still integration under the original target regression law, and PnP_{n} is the target empirical operator with n=ntn=n_{t}. Put Hn=Hℱ​(n−2)H_{n}=H_{\mathcal{F}}(n^{-2}); if Hn=∞H_{n}=\infty, the asserted bound is vacuous.

Step 1: Obtain a single event for every field F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}.

For each F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}, define DF=ℓF−ℓvt0D_{F}=\ell_{F}-\ell_{v_{t}^{0}}, where ℓF​(Wt,Ut,T)=‖F⁡(Wt)−Ut,T‖2\ell_{F}(W_{t},U_{t,T})=\|F(W_{t})-U_{t,T}\|^{2}. By the regression identity in Equation 2.6, P​DF=ℰt​(F)PD_{F}=\mathcal{E}_{t}(F). The conditional version of Equation C.1, with K0=1+KtK_{0}=1+K_{t}, supplies an event Ωx\Omega_{x} of conditional probability at least 1−e−x1-e^{-x} on which

34​ℰt​(F)−bℱ​(x)≤Pn​DF≤54​ℰt​(F)+bℱ​(x),F∈ℱ.\tfrac{3}{4}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F)-b_{\mathcal{F}}(x)\leq P_{n}D_{F}\leq\tfrac{5}{4}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F)+b_{\mathcal{F}}(x),\qquad F\in\mathcal{F}. (C.49)

The event Ωx\Omega_{x} depends on the field class ℱ\mathcal{F} and the observations, but its definition does not involve λ\lambda or the penalty values As​(h)A_{s}(h).

Step 2: Retain the penalty in the empirical comparison.

Fix λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, and write F^λ=Ft,v^λ,h^λ\widehat{F}_{\lambda}=F_{t,\widehat{v}_{\lambda},\widehat{h}_{\lambda}}. For every comparator pair (v,h)∈𝒫(v,h)\in\mathcal{P}, the ϵ\epsilon-minimization property gives

Pn​ℓF^λ+λ​As​(h^λ)≤Pn​ℓFt,v,h+λ​As​(h)+ϵ.P_{n}\ell_{\widehat{F}_{\lambda}}+\lambda A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda})\leq P_{n}\ell_{F_{t,v,h}}+\lambda A_{s}(h)+\epsilon.

Subtracting the common quantity Pn​ℓvt0P_{n}\ell_{v_{t}^{0}}, and then applying the lower and upper bounds in Equation C.49, yields on Ωx\Omega_{x}

34​ℰt​(F^λ)−bℱ​(x)+λ​As​(h^λ)\displaystyle\tfrac{3}{4}\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})-b_{\mathcal{F}}(x)+\lambda A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda})
≤Pn​DF^λ+λ​As​(h^λ)\displaystyle\quad\leq P_{n}D_{\widehat{F}_{\lambda}}+\lambda A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda})
≤Pn​DFt,v,h+λ​As​(h)+ϵ\displaystyle\quad\leq P_{n}D_{F_{t,v,h}}+\lambda A_{s}(h)+\epsilon
≤54​ℰt​(Ft,v,h)+bℱ​(x)+λ​As​(h)+ϵ.\displaystyle\quad\leq\tfrac{5}{4}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h})+b_{\mathcal{F}}(x)+\lambda A_{s}(h)+\epsilon. (C.50)

Move the two copies of bℱ​(x)b_{\mathcal{F}}(x) to the right and multiply by 4/34/3. Equation (C.50) then becomes

ℰt​(F^λ)+4​λ3​As​(h^λ)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})+\tfrac{4\lambda}{3}A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda}) ≤53​ℰt​(Ft,v,h)+4​λ3​As​(h)+83​bℱ​(x)+43​ϵ.\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{5}{3}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h})+\tfrac{4\lambda}{3}A_{s}(h)+\tfrac{8}{3}b_{\mathcal{F}}(x)+\tfrac{4}{3}\epsilon.

Taking the infimum over the pair (v,h)(v,h) proves Equation C.48. This is a pair infimum: if two pairs define the same field but have different penalties, the value As​(h)A_{s}(h) remains attached to its own pair. No identifiability of (v,h)(v,h) from Ft,v,hF_{t,v,h} is assumed.

Since Equation C.49 holds for every F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} on the same event Ωx\Omega_{x}, the preceding algebra is valid there for every λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and every corresponding ϵ\epsilon-minimizer. There is no union bound over λ\lambda, nor any division by λ\lambda. In particular, at λ=0\lambda=0, Equation C.48 reduces directly to

ℰt​(F^0)≤53​inf(v,h)∈𝒫ℰt​(Ft,v,h)+83​bℱ​(x)+43​ϵ.\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{0})\leq\tfrac{5}{3}\inf_{(v,h)\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h})+\tfrac{8}{3}b_{\mathcal{F}}(x)+\tfrac{4}{3}\epsilon.

No limiting argument for F^λ\widehat{F}_{\lambda} as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0 is needed.

Step 3: Integrate the conditional tail for a fixed λ\lambda.

Define the conditional comparator value

Iλ=inf(v,h)∈𝒫{53​ℰt​(Ft,v,h)+4​λ3​As​(h)}.I_{\lambda}=\inf_{(v,h)\in\mathcal{P}}\{\tfrac{5}{3}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h})+\tfrac{4\lambda}{3}A_{s}(h)\}.

If Iλ=∞I_{\lambda}=\infty, the expectation assertion is vacuous. Otherwise put

Zλ\displaystyle Z_{\lambda} ={ℰt​(F^λ)+4​λ3​As​(h^λ)−Iλ−43​ϵ}+,\displaystyle=\big\{\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})+\tfrac{4\lambda}{3}A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda})-I_{\lambda}-\tfrac{4}{3}\epsilon\big\}_{+},
dn\displaystyle d_{n} =8​C​(1+Kt)23​n.\displaystyle=\frac{8C(1+K_{t})^{2}}{3n}.

All quantities in IλI_{\lambda} and HnH_{n} are fixed after conditioning on ℬ\mathcal{B}. The high-probability inequality already proved gives

ℙ⁡{Zλ>dn​(Hn+1+x)∣ℬ}≤e−x,x≥0.\mathbb{P}\{Z_{\lambda}>d_{n}(H_{n}+1+x)\mid\mathcal{B}\}\leq e^{-x},\qquad x\geq 0.

Consequently,

𝔼⁡(Zλ∣ℬ)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Z_{\lambda}\mid\mathcal{B}) ≤dn​(Hn+1)+dn​∫0∞ℙ⁡{Zλ>dn​(Hn+1+x)∣ℬ}​𝑑x\displaystyle\leq d_{n}(H_{n}+1)+d_{n}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\{Z_{\lambda}>d_{n}(H_{n}+1+x)\mid\mathcal{B}\}\,\mathrm{d}x
≤dn​(Hn+2)≤C​(1+Kt)2​{Hn+1}/n.\displaystyle\leq d_{n}(H_{n}+2)\leq C(1+K_{t})^{2}\{H_{n}+1\}/n.

Add Iλ+(4/3)​ϵI_{\lambda}+(4/3)\epsilon to this inequality to obtain the claimed conditional expectation version, with a possibly enlarged universal constant. If the pair infimum IλI_{\lambda} is not attained, its use is justified by taking pairs within an arbitrary positive error of IλI_{\lambda} in Equation C.50 and letting that error tend to zero. The cluster extension follows from the conditional cluster version of Lemma C.1 without changing this algebra. ∎

C.6 Proof of the end-to-end adaptation theorem

Proof of Theorem 2.

The proof uses the source regression bound, a conditional penalized comparison on Es,AE_{s,A}, and a deterministic envelope bound on Es,AcE_{s,A}^{c}. The frozen estimator is analyzed under the same correctability assumption, not under Assumption 3.

Step 1: Derive the source contribution.

By Equation 2.16, the source pair (v^s,h^s)(\widehat{v}_{s},\widehat{h}_{s}) is an ns−2n_{s}^{-2}-minimizer over 𝒱s,Ns×ℋMs\mathcal{V}_{s,N_{s}}\times\mathcal{H}_{M_{s}}. Applying Lemma C.2 using only the source parts of Assumptions 1 and 2, and then using Equation C.29 at (rs,Ds)(r_{s},D_{s}) and (βs,p)(\beta_{s},p), gives

𝔼​𝒟s​(h^s)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{D}_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s}) ≤𝔼​ℰs​(Fs,v^s,h^s)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{s}(F_{s,\widehat{v}_{s},\widehat{h}_{s}})
≤C{ζs2+Ns−2rs/Ds+Ms−2βs/p+(Ns+Ms)​ℓns3ns+ns−2}\displaystyle\leq C\left\{\zeta_{s}^{2}+N_{s}^{-2r_{s}/D_{s}}+M_{s}^{-2\beta_{s}/p}+\frac{(N_{s}+M_{s})\ell_{n_{s}}^{3}}{n_{s}}+n_{s}^{-2}\right\}
≤C​Rs​(ns).\displaystyle\leq CR_{s}(n_{s}). (C.51)

Thus the source bound used here has been proved independently of the calibration and reduced-mean assumptions in Assumption 3.

Step 2: Fix the target-independent information 𝒮\mathscr{S}.

Recall the sigma-field 𝒮=σ⁡(𝒟s,source auxiliary draws,𝒟a)\mathscr{S}=\sigma(\mathscr{D}_{s},\text{source auxiliary draws},\mathscr{D}_{a}) from Section 3.3. Conditional on 𝒮\mathscr{S}, the source function h^s\widehat{h}_{s}, the anchor AsA_{s}, and the pair class

𝒫A=𝒱t,Nt×ℋA​(MA)\mathcal{P}_{A}=\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}}\times\mathcal{H}_{A}(M_{A})

are fixed. The target observations and their auxiliary draws retain their original independent sampling law. Also Es,A={h^s∈ℋgoodA}∈𝒮E_{s,A}=\{\widehat{h}_{s}\in\mathcal{H}_{\rm good}^{A}\}\in\mathscr{S}. The composed field class associated with 𝒫A\mathcal{P}_{A} is ℱA​(Nt,MA)\mathcal{F}_{A}(N_{t},M_{A}), and Equation C.36 gives

HℱA​(Nt,MA)​(nt−2)≤C⁡(Nt+MA)​ℓnt3.H_{\mathcal{F}_{A}(N_{t},M_{A})}(n_{t}^{-2})\leq C(N_{t}+M_{A})\ell_{n_{t}}^{3}. (C.52)

The approximate minimization property Equation 2.20 is precisely the hypothesis of Lemma C.5, with ϵ=nt−2\epsilon=n_{t}^{-2}. Its conditional expectation conclusion, Equation C.52, and λ​As​(h^λ)≥0\lambda A_{s}(\widehat{h}_{\lambda})\geq 0 for 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1 imply

𝔼⁡{ℰt​(F^λ)∣𝒮}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\{\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})\mid\mathscr{S}\} ≤inf(v,h)∈𝒫A{53​ℰt​(Ft,v,h)+4​λ3​As​(h)}\displaystyle\leq\inf_{(v,h)\in\mathcal{P}_{A}}\{\tfrac{5}{3}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h})+\tfrac{4\lambda}{3}A_{s}(h)\}
+C​(Nt+MA)​ℓnt3nt+43​nt−2.\displaystyle\quad+C\frac{(N_{t}+M_{A})\ell_{n_{t}}^{3}}{n_{t}}+\tfrac{4}{3}n_{t}^{-2}. (C.53)

This inequality holds for almost every realization of 𝒮\mathscr{S}, before any restriction to Es,AE_{s,A}.

Step 3: Insert the corrected comparator on Es,AE_{s,A}.

On Es,AE_{s,A}, Lemma C.4 supplies the pair (vNt,hh^s,aMA)∈𝒫A(v_{N_{t}},h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a_{M_{A}}})\in\mathcal{P}_{A}. Its risk and anchor satisfy Equations C.37 and C.38. Substitute these two inequalities into the pair infimum in Equation C.53 to obtain

𝔼{ℰt(F^λ)∣𝒮}≤C{\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\{\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})\mid\mathscr{S}\}\leq C\bigg\{ κA𝒟s(h^s)+ζA2+Nt−2rt/Dt+MA−2βA/qA\displaystyle\kappa_{A}\mathcal{D}_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s})+\zeta_{A}^{2}+N_{t}^{-2r_{t}/D_{t}}+M_{A}^{-2\beta_{A}/q_{A}}
+λδA2+λMA−2βA/qA+(Nt+MA)​ℓnt3nt+nt−2},on Es,A.\displaystyle+\lambda\delta_{A}^{2}+\lambda M_{A}^{-2\beta_{A}/q_{A}}+\frac{(N_{t}+M_{A})\ell_{n_{t}}^{3}}{n_{t}}+n_{t}^{-2}\bigg\},\qquad\text{on }E_{s,A}. (C.54)

In particular, the term λ​δA2\lambda\delta_{A}^{2} comes from the comparator penalty λ​As​(hh^s,aMA)\lambda A_{s}(h_{\widehat{h}_{s},a_{M_{A}}}), not from an asserted lower norm comparison for the anchor. Since 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1,

MA−2βA/qA+λMA−2βA/qA≤2MA−2βA/qA.M_{A}^{-2\beta_{A}/q_{A}}+\lambda M_{A}^{-2\beta_{A}/q_{A}}\leq 2M_{A}^{-2\beta_{A}/q_{A}}.

Thus the residual approximation penalty is absorbed without introducing an inverse power of λ\lambda.

Step 4: Keep the failure-event contribution and balance the target resolutions.

For every training realization, conditional Jensen’s inequality gives ‖vt0​(Wt)‖≤BU,t\|v_{t}^{0}(W_{t})\|\leq B_{U,t}, while membership of the fitted head v^λ\widehat{v}_{\lambda} in 𝒱t,Nt\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}} gives ‖F^λ​(Wt)‖≤BV,t\|\widehat{F}_{\lambda}(W_{t})\|\leq B_{V,t}. Therefore

0≤ℰt​(F^λ)=∫‖F^λ​(w)−vt0​(w)‖2​νt​(𝑑w)≤(BV,t+BU,t)2=Kt2.0\leq\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})=\int\|\widehat{F}_{\lambda}(w)-v_{t}^{0}(w)\|^{2}\nu_{t}(\,\mathrm{d}w)\leq(B_{V,t}+B_{U,t})^{2}=K_{t}^{2}. (C.55)

Let eλ​(𝒮)=𝔼⁡{ℰt​(F^λ)∣𝒮}e_{\lambda}(\mathscr{S})=\mathbb{E}\{\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})\mid\mathscr{S}\}. Since Es,A∈𝒮E_{s,A}\in\mathscr{S}, the tower property gives the exact split

𝔼​ℰt​(F^λ)=𝔼⁡{𝟏​(Es,A)​eλ​(𝒮)}+𝔼⁡{𝟏​(Es,Ac)​eλ​(𝒮)}.\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda})=\mathbb{E}\{\mathbf{1}(E_{s,A})e_{\lambda}(\mathscr{S})\}+\mathbb{E}\{\mathbf{1}(E_{s,A}^{c})e_{\lambda}(\mathscr{S})\}.

Use C.54 on the first event and Equation C.55 on the second. The inequalities ℙ⁡(Es,Ac)≤πs,A\mathbb{P}(E_{s,A}^{c})\leq\pi_{s,A} and 𝔼⁡{𝟏​(Es,A)​𝒟s​(h^s)}≤𝔼​𝒟s​(h^s)\mathbb{E}\{\mathbf{1}(E_{s,A})\mathcal{D}_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s})\}\leq\mathbb{E}\mathcal{D}_{s}(\widehat{h}_{s}) yield

+Nt−2rt/Dt+MA−2βA/qA+(Nt+MA)​ℓnt3nt+nt−2}.\displaystyle+N_{t}^{-2r_{t}/D_{t}}+M_{A}^{-2\beta_{A}/q_{A}}+\frac{(N_{t}+M_{A})\ell_{n_{t}}^{3}}{n_{t}}+n_{t}^{-2}\bigg\}. (C.56)

MA−2βA/qA+MA​ℓnt3nt+nt−2\displaystyle M_{A}^{-2\beta_{A}/q_{A}}+\frac{M_{A}\ell_{n_{t}}^{3}}{n_{t}}+n_{t}^{-2} ≤C​ρβA,qA​(nt).\displaystyle\leq C\rho_{\beta_{A},q_{A}}(n_{t}).

which is Equation 3.20.

+Nt​ℓnt3nt+nt−2},on Es,A.\displaystyle+\frac{N_{t}\ell_{n_{t}}^{3}}{n_{t}}+n_{t}^{-2}\bigg\},\qquad\text{on }E_{s,A}. (C.57)

On Es,AcE_{s,A}^{c}, the proof of Equation C.55 gives ℰt​(F^F)≤Kt2\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{F})\leq K_{t}^{2} as well. Averaging Equation C.57, retaining Kt2​πs,AK_{t}^{2}\pi_{s,A}, and applying Equations C.51 and C.29 therefore yields

𝔼​ℰt​(F^F)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{F}) ≤C⁡{ρrt,Dt​(nt)+κA​Rs​(ns)+ζA2+Kt2​πs,A+Lu,t2​δA2}\displaystyle\leq C\{\rho_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t})+\kappa_{A}R_{s}(n_{s})+\zeta_{A}^{2}+K_{t}^{2}\pi_{s,A}+L_{u,t}^{2}\delta_{A}^{2}\}
=C⁡{ρrt,Dt​(nt)+TA​(ns)+Lu,t2​δA2}.\displaystyle=C\{\rho_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t})+T_{A}(n_{s})+L_{u,t}^{2}\delta_{A}^{2}\}.

𝔼​𝒲t2​(PF^[J],Pt0)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{W}_{t}^{2}(P_{\widehat{F}}^{[J]},P_{t}^{0}) ≤2​CLx,t​𝔼​ℰt​(F^)+2​CEuler​J−2.\displaystyle\leq 2C_{L_{x,t}}\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F})+2C_{\rm Euler}J^{-2}.

Substitution of Equations 3.20 and 3.22 proves Equations 3.21 and 3.23, together with their exact-integration versions.

0≤λnt​δA2≤BR2​λnt≤BR2​min⁡{1,ℜA​(nt)}≤BR2​ℜA​(nt).0\leq\lambda_{n_{t}}\delta_{A}^{2}\leq B_{R}^{2}\lambda_{n_{t}}\leq B_{R}^{2}\min\{1,\mathfrak{R}_{A}(n_{t})\}\leq B_{R}^{2}\mathfrak{R}_{A}(n_{t}).

Insert this inequality into Equation 3.21, and expand ℜA\mathfrak{R}_{A}, TAT_{A}, and RsR_{s} using Equations 3.18, 3.19 and 3.7. The result is exactly Equation 3.25. Every constant used in this proof depends only on the fixed envelopes, architecture constants, smoothness bounds, dimensions, and Lipschitz margins, not on ns,nt,λ,J,δAn_{s},n_{t},\lambda,J,\delta_{A}. ∎

C.7 The information lower bound and strict separation

Lemma C.6 (An endpoint lower bound for frozen context information).

Fix a representation hh and suppose 𝔼​‖Xt‖2<∞\mathbb{E}\|X_{t}\|^{2}<\infty. Let Q(⋅∣z)Q(\cdot\mid z) be any conditional generator with finite second moments whose dependence on zz is only through Ht,h​(z)H_{t,h}(z). Then

𝒲t2​(Q,Pt0)≥ℐt​(h).\mathcal{W}_{t}^{2}(Q,P_{t}^{0})\geq\mathcal{I}_{t}(h). (C.58)

In particular, every exact or Euler-generated field Ft,v,hF_{t,v,h} has this lower bound. For a field with the fixed state Lipschitz budget and the true-flow assumption,

ℰt​(Ft,v,h)≥CLx,t−1​ℐt​(h).\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h})\geq C_{L_{x,t}}^{-1}\mathcal{I}_{t}(h). (C.59)

Both statements hold conditionally on training and after averaging over training when hh is a fitted source representation.

Proof.

Fix the representation hh, and let H=Ht,h​(Zt)H=H_{t,h}(Z_{t}). Define the target conditional mean μt​(z)=𝔼⁡(Xt∣Zt=z)\mu_{t}(z)=\mathbb{E}(X_{t}\mid Z_{t}=z) as in Equation 3.26. By conditional Jensen’s inequality,

𝔼​‖μt​(Zt)‖2≤𝔼​‖Xt‖2<∞.\mathbb{E}\|\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\|X_{t}\|^{2}<\infty. (C.60)

Step 1: Bound a transport cost by the discrepancy of its conditional means.

The assumed factorization of the generator means that there is a probability kernel Q~\widetilde{Q} with Q(⋅∣z)=Q~(⋅∣Ht,h(z))Q(\cdot\mid z)=\widetilde{Q}(\cdot\mid H_{t,h}(z)) for almost every target context zz. Let b⁡(u)=∫y​Q~​(𝑑y∣u)b(u)=\int y\,\widetilde{Q}(\,\mathrm{d}y\mid u) denote its conditional mean. For a fixed such zz and any coupling πz∈Π{Q(⋅∣z),Pt0(⋅∣z)}\pi_{z}\in\Pi\{Q(\cdot\mid z),P_{t}^{0}(\cdot\mid z)\}, Jensen’s inequality under πz\pi_{z} gives

∫‖y−x‖2​πz​(𝑑y,𝑑x)\displaystyle\int\|y-x\|^{2}\pi_{z}(\,\mathrm{d}y,\,\mathrm{d}x) ≥‖∫(y−x)​πz​(𝑑y,𝑑x)‖2\displaystyle\geq\left\|\int(y-x)\pi_{z}(\,\mathrm{d}y,\,\mathrm{d}x)\right\|^{2}
=‖b⁡(Ht,h​(z))−μt​(z)‖2.\displaystyle=\|b(H_{t,h}(z))-\mu_{t}(z)\|^{2}.

The final equality uses the two specified marginals of πz\pi_{z}. Taking the infimum over πz\pi_{z} in Equation 2.8 and then averaging over ZtZ_{t} yields

𝒲t2​(Q,Pt0)≥𝔼​‖b⁡(H)−μt​(Zt)‖2.\mathcal{W}_{t}^{2}(Q,P_{t}^{0})\geq\mathbb{E}\|b(H)-\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\|^{2}. (C.61)

If the left side is infinite, the desired lower bound is immediate, because ℐt​(h)≤𝔼​‖μt​(Zt)‖2<∞\mathcal{I}_{t}(h)\leq\mathbb{E}\|\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\|^{2}<\infty. Otherwise Equation C.61 and Equation C.60 imply

𝔼​‖b⁡(H)‖2≤2​𝔼​‖b⁡(H)−μt​(Zt)‖2+2​𝔼​‖μt​(Zt)‖2<∞.\mathbb{E}\|b(H)\|^{2}\leq 2\mathbb{E}\|b(H)-\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\|\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\|^{2}<\infty.

Thus all conditional projection terms used next are square integrable.

Step 2: Project the target mean onto the frozen context sigma-field σ⁡(H)\sigma(H).

Write μ¯h​(H)=𝔼⁡{μt​(Zt)∣H}\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)=\mathbb{E}\{\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\mid H\}. The vector b​(H)−μ¯h​(H)b(H)-\overline{\mu}_{h}(H) is σ⁡(H)\sigma(H)-measurable, and the defining conditional expectation identity gives

𝔼⁡⟨b⁡(H)−μ¯h​(H),μ¯h​(H)−μt​(Zt)⟩\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\langle b(H)-\overline{\mu}_{h}(H),\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)-\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\right\rangle
=𝔼⁡⟨b⁡(H)−μ¯h​(H),𝔼⁡{μ¯h​(H)−μt​(Zt)∣H}⟩=0.\displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left\langle b(H)-\overline{\mu}_{h}(H),\mathbb{E}\{\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)-\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\mid H\}\right\rangle=0.

Expanding b⁡(H)−μt​(Zt)=[b⁡(H)−μ¯h​(H)]+[μ¯h​(H)−μt​(Zt)]b(H)-\mu_{t}(Z_{t})=[b(H)-\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)]+[\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)-\mu_{t}(Z_{t})] and using this zero cross term proves

𝔼​‖b⁡(H)−μt​(Zt)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|b(H)-\mu_{t}(Z_{t})\|^{2} =𝔼​‖b⁡(H)−μ¯h​(H)‖2+𝔼​‖μt​(Zt)−μ¯h​(H)‖2\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\|b(H)-\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)\|^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|\mu_{t}(Z_{t})-\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)\|^{2}
=𝔼​‖b⁡(H)−μ¯h​(H)‖2+ℐt​(h)≥ℐt​(h).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\|b(H)-\overline{\mu}_{h}(H)\|^{2}+\mathcal{I}_{t}(h)\geq\mathcal{I}_{t}(h). (C.62)

Here the second equality is the definition Equation 3.26. Combining Equations C.61 and C.62 proves Equation C.58.

Step 3: Verify the required factorization for exact and Euler-generated laws.

Fix a feasible head vv and a base initial value gg. For Ft,v,hF_{t,v,h}, the exact equation Equation 2.7 reads

X˙​(τ)=v⁡(X⁡(τ),h⁡(z0),zc,τ),X⁡(0)=g.\dot{X}(\tau)=v(X(\tau),h(z_{0}),z_{c},\tau),\qquad X(0)=g.

If Ht,h​(z)=Ht,h​(z′)H_{t,h}(z)=H_{t,h}(z^{\prime}), then both the right-hand side and the initial condition are identical for contexts zz and z′z^{\prime}. Uniqueness of the fitted ODE, supplied by its global state-Lipschitz bound, implies identical exact endpoints. More explicitly, for each reduced context u=(u0,uc)u=(u_{0},u_{c}), the solution of X˙=v⁡(X,u0,uc,τ)\dot{X}=v(X,u_{0},u_{c},\tau) defines a measurable endpoint map φv​(g,u)\varphi_{v}(g,u). The exact generator is the pushforward of γt\gamma_{t} by g↦φv​(g,Ht,h​(z))g\mapsto\varphi_{v}(g,H_{t,h}(z)), and therefore depends on zz only through Ht,h​(z)H_{t,h}(z).

For Euler generation, define the iterates explicitly by

x0​(g,z)=g,xk+1​(g,z)=xk​(g,z)+1J​v​(xk​(g,z),h⁡(z0),zc,k/J),0≤k<J.x_{0}(g,z)=g,\qquad x_{k+1}(g,z)=x_{k}(g,z)+\frac{1}{J}v(x_{k}(g,z),h(z_{0}),z_{c},k/J),\quad 0\leq k<J. (C.63)

An induction on kk in Equation C.63 shows that xk​(g,z)=xk​(g,z′)x_{k}(g,z)=x_{k}(g,z^{\prime}) whenever Ht,h​(z)=Ht,h​(z′)H_{t,h}(z)=H_{t,h}(z^{\prime}). Hence the Euler endpoint law has the same reduced-context factorization for every J≥1J\geq 1. The base law γt\gamma_{t} is context independent by the model definition. Both endpoint laws have finite second moments: boundedness of the head vv implies

‖X⁡(1)‖≤‖Gt‖+BV,t,‖xJ​(Gt,z)‖≤‖Gt‖+BV,t,\|X(1)\|\leq\|G_{t}\|+B_{V,t},\qquad\|x_{J}(G_{t},z)\|\leq\|G_{t}\|+B_{V,t},

so their second moments are at most 2​𝔼​‖Gt‖2+2​BV,t22\mathbb{E}\|G_{t}\|^{2}+2B_{V,t}^{2}. They are therefore eligible for Equation C.58.

Step 4: Derive the velocity lower bound using the exact flow.

Apply Equation C.58 to the exact endpoint law PFt,v,hP_{F_{t,v,h}}, and then use Equation A.2 under the stated true-flow assumption. The resulting inequalities are

ℐt​(h)≤𝒲t2​(PFt,v,h,Pt0)≤CLx,t​ℰt​(Ft,v,h).\mathcal{I}_{t}(h)\leq\mathcal{W}_{t}^{2}(P_{F_{t,v,h}},P_{t}^{0})\leq C_{L_{x,t}}\mathcal{E}_{t}(F_{t,v,h}). (C.64)

The constant CLx,t>0C_{L_{x,t}}>0 is given explicitly by Equation A.3. Division by this constant proves Equation C.59. The use of the exact-flow inequality is important: no subtraction of an Euler discretization remainder is needed to obtain the velocity lower bound.

Step 5: Condition on fitted functions and average over training.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} contain all source and target fitting randomness, and let the evaluation observation (Xt,Zt)(X_{t},Z_{t}) and base draw GtG_{t} be fresh and independent of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Conditional on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the fitted functions are fixed and the evaluation law is the original target law. Thus Steps 1–4 apply for almost every training realization, even when the fitted head uses the target training sample. For h=h^sh=\widehat{h}_{s}, integration over 𝒯\mathcal{T} gives a lower bound of 𝔼​ℐt​(h^s)=ℐF​(ns)\mathbb{E}\mathcal{I}_{t}(\widehat{h}_{s})=\mathcal{I}_{F}(n_{s}) for either expected endpoint risk, and CLx,t−1​ℐF​(ns)C_{L_{x,t}}^{-1}\mathcal{I}_{F}(n_{s}) for the expected velocity risk. The equality with ℐF​(ns)\mathcal{I}_{F}(n_{s}) uses Equation 3.27 and the fact that h^s\widehat{h}_{s} is determined solely by source training. ∎

Proof of Corollary 3.1.

All limits below are along the sequence in Equation 3.28, with δA>0\delta_{A}>0. To distinguish the deterministic expected risks from the fitted fields, write

RF[J]\displaystyle R_{F}^{[J]} =𝔼​𝒲t2​(PF^F[J],Pt0),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{W}_{t}^{2}(P_{\widehat{F}_{F}}^{[J]},P_{t}^{0}), Rλ[J]\displaystyle R_{\lambda}^{[J]} =𝔼​𝒲t2​(PF^λ[J],Pt0),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{W}_{t}^{2}(P_{\widehat{F}_{\lambda}}^{[J]},P_{t}^{0}),
VF\displaystyle V_{F} =𝔼​ℰt​(F^F),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{F}), Vλ\displaystyle V_{\lambda} =𝔼​ℰt​(F^λ).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{E}_{t}(\widehat{F}_{\lambda}).

Define the nonnegative deterministic remainder ratio

rgap=ℜA​(nt)+TA​(ns)+J−2δA2.r_{\rm gap}=\frac{\mathfrak{R}_{A}(n_{t})+T_{A}(n_{s})+J^{-2}}{\delta_{A}^{2}}. (C.65)

The second condition in Equation 3.28 states exactly that rgap→0r_{\rm gap}\to 0.

Step 1: Match the frozen endpoint risk to δA2\delta_{A}^{2}.

For each training realization, the Euler endpoint law of F^F=Ft,v^F,h^s\widehat{F}_{F}=F_{t,\widehat{v}_{F},\widehat{h}_{s}} uses context only through Ht,h^sH_{t,\widehat{h}_{s}}. The conditional assertion of Lemma C.6, averaged over training, gives

RF[J]≥𝔼​ℐt​(h^s)=ℐF​(ns)≥c0​δA2.R_{F}^{[J]}\geq\mathbb{E}\mathcal{I}_{t}(\widehat{h}_{s})=\mathcal{I}_{F}(n_{s})\geq c_{0}\delta_{A}^{2}. (C.66)

The last inequality is the first condition in Equation 3.28, and it holds for every JJ. In particular, RF[J]>0R_{F}^{[J]}>0 along the sequence.

For the upper bound, Equation 3.23 gives

RF[J]\displaystyle R_{F}^{[J]} ≤C⁡{ρrt,Dt​(nt)+TA​(ns)+J−2+Lu,t2​δA2}\displaystyle\leq C\{\rho_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t})+T_{A}(n_{s})+J^{-2}+L_{u,t}^{2}\delta_{A}^{2}\}
≤C⁡{rgap+Lu,t2}​δA2.\displaystyle\leq C\{r_{\rm gap}+L_{u,t}^{2}\}\delta_{A}^{2}. (C.67)

Here ρrt,Dt​(nt)≤ℜA​(nt)\rho_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t})\leq\mathfrak{R}_{A}(n_{t}) by Equation 3.18. For all sufficiently large sample sizes, rgap≤1r_{\rm gap}\leq 1, so Equations C.66 and C.67 imply

c0​δA2≤RF[J]≤C⁡(1+Lu,t2)​δA2.c_{0}\delta_{A}^{2}\leq R_{F}^{[J]}\leq C(1+L_{u,t}^{2})\delta_{A}^{2}.

Both constants are fixed along the sequence. This proves the two-sided statement Equation 3.29.

Step 2: Compare the adaptive endpoint risk with the positive frozen lower bound.

Equation (3.21) and the definition Equation C.65 give

0≤Rλ[J]≤C⁡{ℜA​(nt)+TA​(ns)+J−2+λ​δA2}=C⁡(rgap+λ)​δA2.0\leq R_{\lambda}^{[J]}\leq C\{\mathfrak{R}_{A}(n_{t})+T_{A}(n_{s})+J^{-2}+\lambda\delta_{A}^{2}\}=C(r_{\rm gap}+\lambda)\delta_{A}^{2}. (C.68)

The conditions rgap→0r_{\rm gap}\to 0 and λ→0\lambda\to 0 imply Rλ[J]=o⁡(δA2)R_{\lambda}^{[J]}=o(\delta_{A}^{2}). More explicitly, division by Equation C.66 gives

0≤Rλ[J]RF[J]≤Cc0​(rgap+λ)⟶0.0\leq\frac{R_{\lambda}^{[J]}}{R_{F}^{[J]}}\leq\frac{C}{c_{0}}(r_{\rm gap}+\lambda)\longrightarrow 0.

This proves Equation 3.30 by a lower bound on the denominator, rather than by comparing two upper bounds.

Step 3: Establish the exact-flow and velocity-risk assertions.

For exact integration, define RF,RλR_{F},R_{\lambda} by replacing each numerical law PF^[J]P_{\widehat{F}}^{[J]} with PF^P_{\widehat{F}}, and replace rgapr_{\rm gap} by

rgapexact={ℜA​(nt)+TA​(ns)}/δA2.r_{\rm gap}^{\rm exact}=\{\mathfrak{R}_{A}(n_{t})+T_{A}(n_{s})\}/\delta_{A}^{2}.

The exact-endpoint part of Lemma C.6 supplies RF≥c0​δA2R_{F}\geq c_{0}\delta_{A}^{2}, and the exact-integration versions of Equations 3.21 and 3.23 supply the same upper bounds with rgapexactr_{\rm gap}^{\rm exact} and no Euler term. Thus the exact-flow conclusions follow under the stated corresponding condition with J−2J^{-2} omitted.

For velocity risk, averaging Equation C.59 gives

VF≥CLx,t−1​ℐF​(ns)≥(c0/CLx,t)​δA2>0.V_{F}\geq C_{L_{x,t}}^{-1}\mathcal{I}_{F}(n_{s})\geq(c_{0}/C_{L_{x,t}})\delta_{A}^{2}>0.

0≤VλVF\displaystyle 0\leq\frac{V_{\lambda}}{V_{F}} ≤C​CLx,tc0​{ℜA​(nt)+TA​(ns)δA2+λ}\displaystyle\leq\frac{CC_{L_{x,t}}}{c_{0}}\left\{\frac{\mathfrak{R}_{A}(n_{t})+T_{A}(n_{s})}{\delta_{A}^{2}}+\lambda\right\}
≤C​CLx,tc0​(rgap+λ)⟶0.\displaystyle\leq\frac{CC_{L_{x,t}}}{c_{0}}(r_{\rm gap}+\lambda)\longrightarrow 0.

For the exact-integration formulation use rgapexactr_{\rm gap}^{\rm exact} in the last line. This proves the claimed ratio of expected flow-matching excess risks. ∎

C.8 Proof of the non-transfer theorem

Proof of Theorem 3.

The target-only estimator in Equation 3.31 fits both the head v^NT\widehat{v}_{\rm NT} and the encoder h^NT\widehat{h}_{\rm NT} on the same target observations. We therefore apply the regression oracle to a joint class, not to a class obtained by conditioning on h^NT\widehat{h}_{\rm NT}.

Step 1: Identify the target-only class and its smooth comparator.

The deterministic class fixed before target training is

ℱNT={Ft,v,h:v∈𝒱t,Nt,h∈ℋMt},Nt=Krt,Dt(nt),Mt=Kβt,p(nt).\mathcal{F}_{\rm NT}=\{F_{t,v,h}:v\in\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}},\ h\in\mathcal{H}_{M_{t}}\},\qquad N_{t}=K_{r_{t},D_{t}}(n_{t}),\quad M_{t}=K_{\beta_{t},p}(n_{t}).

The target part of Assumption 2 supplies the functions ht,0h_{t,0} and gt,0g_{t,0}, with structural error ζt2\zeta_{t}^{2} as defined by Equation 3.1. By Lemma B.2, choose the feasible approximants hMt∈ℋMth_{M_{t}}\in\mathcal{H}_{M_{t}} and vt,Nt∈𝒱t,Ntv_{t,N_{t}}\in\mathcal{V}_{t,N_{t}} so that

∥hMt−ht,0∥∞≤CMt−βt/p,∥vt,Nt−gt,0∥∞,𝒦t≤CNt−rt/Dt.\|h_{M_{t}}-h_{t,0}\|_{\infty}\leq CM_{t}^{-\beta_{t}/p},\qquad\|v_{t,N_{t}}-g_{t,0}\|_{\infty,\mathcal{K}_{t}}\leq CN_{t}^{-r_{t}/D_{t}}.

For the comparator field, add and subtract the two smooth-head compositions to obtain

For each hh in a declared class, let Qh=(St,T,h⁡(Zt,0),Zt,c,T)Q_{h}=(S_{t,T},h(Z_{t,0}),Z_{t,c},T), with law μh\mu_{h}. Suppose μh\mu_{h} has a density qhq_{h} on 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t}, and its vector first-moment measure has a density bhb_{h}, meaning

Differentiating qh​qh−1=1q_{h}q_{h}^{-1}=1 gives, for a nonzero multi-index ν\nu with |ν|≤k|\nu|\leq k,

Dν(qh−1)=−qh−1∑0<ω≤ν(νω)DωqhDν−ω(qh−1).D^{\nu}(q_{h}^{-1})=-q_{h}^{-1}\sum_{0<\omega\leq\nu}\binom{\nu}{\omega}D^{\omega}q_{h}\,D^{\nu-\omega}(q_{h}^{-1}).

The original conditional expectation has norm at most BU,tB_{U,t} almost everywhere. The continuous ratio version agrees with it almost everywhere. Since qh≥cqq_{h}\geq c_{q}, every relatively open subset of the rectangle has positive μh\mu_{h}-measure. Continuity therefore extends the norm bound to the whole rectangle, including its boundary. The uniform first-derivative bounds bound each block Lipschitz constant; strictly larger budgets supply fixed margins. ∎

The first has squared norm at most CN−2rt/DtCN^{-2r_{t}/D_{t}}, the second at most Lu,t2​𝔼Zt​‖h^s−ht,0‖2L_{u,t}^{2}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}}\|\widehat{h}_{s}-h_{t,0}\|^{2}, and the third has squared norm ζt2\zeta_{t}^{2}. The squared three-term triangle inequality and Equation D.8 give the desired bound on Qt,N​(h^s)Q_{t,N}(\widehat{h}_{s}) on EsE_{s}. On its complement the zero-head comparator bounds the profile by BU,t2B_{U,t}^{2}. Averaging proves Equation D.9. The frozen proof uses Assumption 3 only through the profile bound in Lemma C.3. Replacing that bound by Equation D.9, and using the same source rate, proves Equation D.10. No deficiency term is added again: Equation D.9 already bounds the full profile risk. ∎

Appendix E Endpoint validation: detailed guarantees and proofs

This appendix proves the results used in Section 4. We retain the notation n=nvaln=n_{\rm val}, d=dtd=d_{t}, and Ae=DeυA_{\rm e}=D_{\rm e}^{\upsilon} from that section.

E.1 Support, deployment, and a deterministic selection principle

Lemma E.1 (Bounded endpoint support and solver changes).

Under the bounded-state part of Assumption 1 and the path condition Equation 2.2, Gt,Xt∈[−Kx,t,Kx,t]dG_{t},X_{t}\in[-K_{x,t},K_{x,t}]^{d} almost surely. Every exact or Euler endpoint of a field bounded by BV,tB_{V,t} lies in [−Kx,t−BV,t,Kx,t+BV,t]d[-K_{x,t}-B_{V,t},K_{x,t}+B_{V,t}]^{d} almost surely. More generally, suppose two endpoint dictionaries Qm,Q~mQ_{m},\widetilde{Q}_{m} satisfy, on a common support of diameter DeD_{\rm e}, supzW2​(Qm,z,Q~m,z)≤ϵsol\sup_{z}W_{2}(Q_{m,z},\widetilde{Q}_{m,z})\leq\epsilon_{\rm sol} for every mm. Then

supm|ℛW​(Qm)−ℛW​(Q~m)|≤2​De​ϵsol.\sup_{m}|\mathcal{R}_{\rm W}(Q_{m})-\mathcal{R}_{\rm W}(\widetilde{Q}_{m})|\leq 2D_{\rm e}\epsilon_{\rm sol}. (E.1)

For exact versus Euler integration under Lemma A.3, one may take ϵsol=CEuler/minm⁡Jm\epsilon_{\rm sol}=\sqrt{C_{\rm Euler}}/\min_{m}J_{m}. Thus validating and deploying the same numerical laws avoids a separate solver-change remainder.

Proof.

The interpolation path τ↦St,τ=Ψt,τ​(Gt,Xt)\tau\mapsto S_{t,\tau}=\Psi_{t,\tau}(G_{t},X_{t}) is determined by 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}. The interpolation time T∼Unif⁡[0,1]T\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1] is independent of 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}, by the sampling construction preceding Equation 2.2. The bounded-state assertion in Assumption 1 and Tonelli’s theorem therefore give

0\displaystyle 0 =ℙ⁡(St,T∉Ct)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(S_{t,T}\notin C_{t})
=𝔼[𝔼{𝟏(St,T∉Ct)∣𝒢t}]=𝔼∫01𝟏{St,τ∉Ct}dτ.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbb{E}\{\mathbf{1}(S_{t,T}\notin C_{t})\mid\mathcal{G}_{t}\}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{1}\mathbf{1}\{S_{t,\tau}\notin C_{t}\}\,\mathrm{d}\tau. (E.2)

Define the nonnegative random variable It=∫01𝟏{St,τ∉Ct}dτI_{t}=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbf{1}\{S_{t,\tau}\notin C_{t}\}\,\mathrm{d}\tau. Equation (E.2) implies It=0I_{t}=0 almost surely. Fix a realization ω0∈Ωt0\omega_{0}\in\Omega_{t}^{0}. Suppose, for a contradiction, that St,τ0∉CtS_{t,\tau_{0}}\notin C_{t} for some τ0∈[0,1]\tau_{0}\in[0,1]. Substituting τ=0,1\tau=0,1 in Equation 2.2 proves

Lemma E.2 (Uniform contrasts, selection, and safe switching).

Let R1,…,RM∈[0,H]R_{1},\ldots,R_{M}\in[0,H] be fixed risks, let bb be a common offset, and suppose an event EE satisfies

maxm⁡|l^m−(Rm+b)|≤ϵ.\max_{m}|\widehat{l}_{m}-(R_{m}+b)|\leq\epsilon. (E.8)

Let m^\widehat{m} minimize l^m\widehat{l}_{m}. For a fixed baseline index m0m_{0}, return m^\widehat{m} if l^m0−l^m^>2​ϵ\widehat{l}_{m_{0}}-\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}}>2\epsilon, and otherwise return m0m_{0}; call the resulting index m^safe\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}. On EE,

Rm^≤minm⁡Rm+2​ϵ,Rm^safe≤Rm0,Rm^safe≤minm⁡Rm+4​ϵ.R_{\widehat{m}}\leq\min_{m}R_{m}+2\epsilon,\qquad R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}\leq R_{m_{0}},\qquad R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}\leq\min_{m}R_{m}+4\epsilon. (E.9)

If Rm0−minm⁡Rm>4​ϵR_{m_{0}}-\min_{m}R_{m}>4\epsilon, switching occurs on EE. If ℙ⁡(Ec)≤δ\mathbb{P}(E^{c})\leq\delta, then 𝔼​Rm^≤minm⁡Rm+2​ϵ+H​δ\mathbb{E}R_{\widehat{m}}\leq\min_{m}R_{m}+2\epsilon+H\delta and 𝔼​Rm^safe≤Rm0+H​δ\mathbb{E}R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}\leq R_{m_{0}}+H\delta. The same statements hold conditionally on information fixing the risks.

Proof.

Let R∗=min1≤m≤M⁡RmR_{*}=\min_{1\leq m\leq M}R_{m}, and choose an index m∗∈arg​min1≤m≤M⁡Rmm_{*}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{1\leq m\leq M}R_{m} by a fixed tie rule. Define the switching event

Asw={l^m0−l^m^>2ϵ}.A_{\rm sw}=\{\widehat{l}_{m_{0}}-\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}}>2\epsilon\}.

The index m^safe\widehat{m}_{\rm safe} equals m^\widehat{m} on AswA_{\rm sw} and m0m_{0} on AswcA_{\rm sw}^{c}. All comparisons in Steps 1–3 are made on the event EE in Equation E.8.

Step 1: the unguarded oracle inequality. For every index mm, Equation (E.8) implies l^m−b−ϵ≤Rm≤l^m−b+ϵ\widehat{l}_{m}-b-\epsilon\leq R_{m}\leq\widehat{l}_{m}-b+\epsilon. The simultaneous nature of these inequalities permits their use at the random index m^\widehat{m}. Since l^m^≤l^m∗\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}}\leq\widehat{l}_{m_{*}},

Rm^≤l^m^−b+ϵ≤l^m∗−b+ϵ≤R∗+2​ϵ.R_{\widehat{m}}\leq\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}}-b+\epsilon\leq\widehat{l}_{m_{*}}-b+\epsilon\leq R_{*}+2\epsilon. (E.10)

This is the first inequality in Equation E.9.

Step 2: the baseline and oracle inequalities for m^safe\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}. On E∩AswE\cap A_{\rm sw}, the definition of AswA_{\rm sw} and Equation E.8 give

Rm^safe=Rm^≤l^m^−b+ϵ<l^m0−b−ϵ≤Rm0.R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}=R_{\widehat{m}}\leq\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}}-b+\epsilon<\widehat{l}_{m_{0}}-b-\epsilon\leq R_{m_{0}}. (E.11)

On E∩AswcE\cap A_{\rm sw}^{c}, the returned index is m0m_{0}, so Rm^safe=Rm0R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}=R_{m_{0}}. These two cases prove the second inequality in Equation E.9.

For the oracle comparison on E∩AswE\cap A_{\rm sw}, Equation (E.10) gives Rm^safe≤R∗+2​ϵ≤R∗+4​ϵR_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}\leq R_{*}+2\epsilon\leq R_{*}+4\epsilon. For the remaining event E∩AswcE\cap A_{\rm sw}^{c}, the no-switch inequality is l^m0≤l^m^+2​ϵ\widehat{l}_{m_{0}}\leq\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}}+2\epsilon. Consequently

Rm^safe=Rm0\displaystyle R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}=R_{m_{0}} ≤l^m0−b+ϵ\displaystyle\leq\widehat{l}_{m_{0}}-b+\epsilon
≤l^m^−b+3​ϵ≤l^m∗−b+3​ϵ≤R∗+4​ϵ.\displaystyle\leq\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}}-b+3\epsilon\leq\widehat{l}_{m_{*}}-b+3\epsilon\leq R_{*}+4\epsilon. (E.12)

Combining the two cases proves the third inequality in Equation E.9.

Step 3: sufficient population improvement for switching. Suppose Rm0−R∗>4​ϵR_{m_{0}}-R_{*}>4\epsilon. On EE,

l^m0−l^m^\displaystyle\widehat{l}_{m_{0}}-\widehat{l}_{\widehat{m}} ≥l^m0−l^m∗\displaystyle\geq\widehat{l}_{m_{0}}-\widehat{l}_{m_{*}}
≥(Rm0+b−ϵ)−(R∗+b+ϵ)=Rm0−R∗−2​ϵ>2​ϵ.\displaystyle\geq(R_{m_{0}}+b-\epsilon)-(R_{*}+b+\epsilon)=R_{m_{0}}-R_{*}-2\epsilon>2\epsilon. (E.13)

Thus E⊆AswE\subseteq A_{\rm sw} under the stated improvement condition. The strict inequalities in Equations E.11 and E.13 match the strict switching threshold 2​ϵ2\epsilon; no assertion of switching is needed at equality.

Step 4: expectation inequalities and conditioning. The bounds 0≤Rm≤H0\leq R_{m}\leq H imply, on every realization, Rm^−R∗≤HR_{\widehat{m}}-R_{*}\leq H and Rm^safe−Rm0≤HR_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}-R_{m_{0}}\leq H. Split the first excess risk over EE and EcE^{c}, and use Equation E.10:

𝔼​Rm^−R∗\displaystyle\mathbb{E}R_{\widehat{m}}-R_{*} =𝔼⁡{(Rm^−R∗)​𝟏​(E)}+𝔼⁡{(Rm^−R∗)​𝟏​(Ec)}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\{(R_{\widehat{m}}-R_{*})\mathbf{1}(E)\}+\mathbb{E}\{(R_{\widehat{m}}-R_{*})\mathbf{1}(E^{c})\}
≤2​ϵ​ℙ​(E)+H​ℙ​(Ec)≤2​ϵ+H​δ.\displaystyle\leq 2\epsilon\mathbb{P}(E)+H\mathbb{P}(E^{c})\leq 2\epsilon+H\delta.

The baseline inequality proved in Step 2 similarly gives

𝔼​Rm^safe−Rm0\displaystyle\mathbb{E}R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}-R_{m_{0}} =𝔼⁡{(Rm^safe−Rm0)​𝟏​(E)}+𝔼⁡{(Rm^safe−Rm0)​𝟏​(Ec)}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\{(R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}-R_{m_{0}})\mathbf{1}(E)\}+\mathbb{E}\{(R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}-R_{m_{0}})\mathbf{1}(E^{c})\}
≤0+H​ℙ​(Ec)≤H​δ.\displaystyle\leq 0+H\mathbb{P}(E^{c})\leq H\delta.

These are the two claimed expectation bounds.

For the conditional statements, let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be information fixing (R1,…,RM)(R_{1},\ldots,R_{M}), the offset bb, the baseline index m0m_{0}, and the chosen bounds H,ϵ,δH,\epsilon,\delta. If ℙ⁡(Ec∣𝒜)≤δ\mathbb{P}(E^{c}\mid\mathcal{A})\leq\delta almost surely, the same pathwise inequalities Equations E.10, E.11, E.12 and E.13 hold. Taking conditional expectations in the preceding decompositions therefore yields

𝔼⁡(Rm^∣𝒜)≤R∗+2​ϵ+H​δ,𝔼⁡(Rm^safe∣𝒜)≤Rm0+H​δ.\mathbb{E}(R_{\widehat{m}}\mid\mathcal{A})\leq R_{*}+2\epsilon+H\delta,\qquad\mathbb{E}(R_{\widehat{m}_{\rm safe}}\mid\mathcal{A})\leq R_{m_{0}}+H\delta.

E.2 The conditional energy identity and its Hilbert geometry

Lemma E.3 (Energy scores as bounded squared Hilbert losses).

For υ∈(0,2)\upsilon\in(0,2), there is a real separable Hilbert space ℍυ\mathbb{H}_{\upsilon} and a continuous map ϕ:𝒦e→ℍυ\phi:\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}\to\mathbb{H}_{\upsilon} such that

‖ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(y)‖ℍυ2=‖x−y‖υ.\|\phi(x)-\phi(y)\|_{\mathbb{H}_{\upsilon}}^{2}=\|x-y\|^{\upsilon}. (E.14)

For μQ=∫ϕ⁡(y)​Q​(𝑑y)\mu_{Q}=\int\phi(y)Q(\,\mathrm{d}y),

Sυ​(Q,x)\displaystyle S_{\upsilon}(Q,x) =‖μQ−ϕ⁡(x)‖ℍυ2,\displaystyle=\|\mu_{Q}-\phi(x)\|_{\mathbb{H}_{\upsilon}}^{2}, (E.15)
12​𝖣υ​(P,Q)\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\mathsf{D}_{\upsilon}(P,Q) =‖μP−μQ‖ℍυ2.\displaystyle=\|\mu_{P}-\mu_{Q}\|_{\mathbb{H}_{\upsilon}}^{2}. (E.16)

On the common support, 0≤Sυ​(Q,x)≤Ae0\leq S_{\upsilon}(Q,x)\leq A_{\rm e} and 0≤𝖣υ​(P,Q)/2≤Ae0\leq\mathsf{D}_{\upsilon}(P,Q)/2\leq A_{\rm e}. Moreover μP=μQ\mu_{P}=\mu_{Q} if and only if P=QP=Q. The conditional identity Equation 4.5 follows, and ℛE,υ\mathcal{R}_{{\rm E},\upsilon} is convex under mixtures of probability kernels. For fixed xx, the function μ↦exp⁡{−η​‖μ−ϕ⁡(x)‖2}\mu\mapsto\exp\{-\eta\|\mu-\phi(x)\|^{2}\} is concave on the convex hull of the embeddings of supported probability laws whenever 0<η≤1/(2​Ae)0<\eta\leq 1/(2A_{\rm e}).

Proof.

Fix d=dt≥1d=d_{t}\geq 1, υ∈(0,2)\upsilon\in(0,2), and the compact endpoint support 𝒦e\mathcal{K}_{\rm e} from Assumption 5. Throughout this proof, all probability laws P,QP,Q under discussion are supported on 𝒦e\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}.

Step 1: construct the Hilbert space ℍυ\mathbb{H}_{\upsilon} and the feature map ϕ\phi. For t=(t1,…,td)∈ℝdt=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define

Id,υ=∫ℝd1−cos⁡(t1)‖t‖d+υ​𝑑t.I_{d,\upsilon}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1-\cos(t_{1})}{\|t\|^{d+\upsilon}}\,\mathrm{d}t. (E.17)

The value assigned to the integrand at t=0t=0 does not affect this Lebesgue integral. Let σd−1\sigma_{d-1} be the surface measure of the unit sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. On {∥t∥≤1}\{\|t\|\leq 1\}, 1−cos⁡(t1)≤t12/2≤‖t‖2/21-\cos(t_{1})\leq t_{1}^{2}/2\leq\|t\|^{2}/2; on {∥t∥>1}\{\|t\|>1\}, 1−cos⁡(t1)≤21-\cos(t_{1})\leq 2. Polar integration gives

Id,υ\displaystyle I_{d,\upsilon} ≤σd−12​∫01r1−υ​𝑑r+2​σd−1​∫1∞r−1−υ​𝑑r\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sigma_{d-1}}{2}\int_{0}^{1}r^{1-\upsilon}\,\mathrm{d}r+2\sigma_{d-1}\int_{1}^{\infty}r^{-1-\upsilon}\,\mathrm{d}r

For a∈ℝd∖{0}a\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}, choose an orthogonal matrix OO with O​e1=a/‖a‖Oe_{1}=a/\|a\|, where e1e_{1} is the first coordinate vector. For a=0a=0, both sides of Equation E.18 are zero.

Choose x∘∈𝒦ex_{\circ}\in\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}, and define the measure ω\omega, the real Hilbert space ℍ\mathbb{H}, and the map ϕ\phi by

ω⁡(d​t)\displaystyle\omega(\,\mathrm{d}t) =‖t‖−d−υ2​Id,υ​d​t,ℍ=ℍυ=L2​(ω,ℝ2),\displaystyle=\frac{\|t\|^{-d-\upsilon}}{2I_{d,\upsilon}}\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\mathbb{H}=\mathbb{H}_{\upsilon}=L_{2}(\omega;\mathbb{R}^{2}), (E.19)

For real numbers r,sr,s, (cos⁡r−cos⁡s)2+(sin⁡r−sin⁡s)2=2​{1−cos⁡(r−s)}(\cos r-\cos s)^{2}+(\sin r-\sin s)^{2}=2\{1-\cos(r-s)\}. Using this identity and Equation E.18,

h⁡(s)=exp⁡{−η​‖μs−ϕ⁡(x)‖ℍ2},0≤s≤1.h(s)=\exp\{-\eta\|\mu_{s}-\phi(x)\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\},\qquad 0\leq s\leq 1.

≤h⁡(s)​{4​η2​‖μs−ϕ⁡(x)‖ℍ2−2​η}​‖ξ‖ℍ2\displaystyle\leq h(s)\{4\eta^{2}\|\mu_{s}-\phi(x)\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}-2\eta\}\|\xi\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}
≤2​η​h​(s)​(2​η​Ae−1)​‖ξ‖ℍ2≤0.\displaystyle\leq 2\eta h(s)(2\eta A_{\rm e}-1)\|\xi\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\leq 0. (E.28)

E.3 Simulation scores: unbiasedness and a conditional exponential bound

Lemma E.4 (Unbiased energy simulation and its exponential error).

Condition on a context, an observed endpoint xx, and a supported law QQ. For B≥2B\geq 2 independent draws from QQ, the score S^\widehat{S} in Equation 4.6 satisfies

𝔼⁡(S^∣Q,x)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\widehat{S}\mid Q,x) =Sυ(Q,x),−Ae/2≤S^≤Ae,\displaystyle=S_{\upsilon}(Q,x),\qquad-A_{\rm e}/2\leq\widehat{S}\leq A_{\rm e}, (E.29)
𝔼[exp{t(S^−Sυ(Q,x))}∣Q,x]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\{t(\widehat{S}-S_{\upsilon}(Q,x))\}\mid Q,x\right] ≤exp⁡{t2​Ae2/(2​B)},t∈ℝ.\displaystyle\leq\exp\{t^{2}A_{\rm e}^{2}/(2B)\},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}. (E.30)

Replacing B⁡(B−1)B(B-1) in the pairwise term by B2B^{2} instead gives conditional mean

Sυ​(Q,x)+12​B​𝔼Y,Y′∼Q​‖Y−Y′‖υ.S_{\upsilon}(Q,x)+\frac{1}{2B}\mathbb{E}_{Y,Y^{\prime}\sim Q}\|Y-Y^{\prime}\|^{\upsilon}. (E.31)

This candidate-dependent term must not be discarded when comparing the original generator laws.

Proof.

Fix a context zz, the observed endpoint x∈𝒦ex\in\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}, and the supported probability law QQ. All expectations in this proof are over Y1,…,YB∼iidQY_{1},\ldots,Y_{B}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm iid}}{{\sim}}Q, unless another probability law is explicitly introduced. Define

ρυ​(y,y′)=‖y−y′‖υ,a⁡(Q,x)=∫ρυ​(y,x)​Q​(𝑑y),p⁡(Q)=∬ρυ​(y,y′)​Q​(𝑑y)​Q​(d​y′).\rho_{\upsilon}(y,y^{\prime})=\|y-y^{\prime}\|^{\upsilon},\qquad a(Q,x)=\int\rho_{\upsilon}(y,x)Q(\,\mathrm{d}y),\qquad p(Q)=\iint\rho_{\upsilon}(y,y^{\prime})Q(\,\mathrm{d}y)Q(\,\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}).

By Assumption 5, 0≤ρυ​(y,y′)≤Ae0\leq\rho_{\upsilon}(y,y^{\prime})\leq A_{\rm e} on 𝒦e×𝒦e\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}\times\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}. In this notation, Equation 4.2 reads Sυ​(Q,x)=a⁡(Q,x)−p⁡(Q)/2S_{\upsilon}(Q,x)=a(Q,x)-p(Q)/2.

Step 1: compute the mean and range of S^\widehat{S}. For each bb, 𝔼{ρυ(Yb,x)∣Q,x}=a(Q,x)\mathbb{E}\{\rho_{\upsilon}(Y_{b},x)\mid Q,x\}=a(Q,x). For each ordered pair (b,b′)(b,b^{\prime}) with b≠b′b\neq b^{\prime}, independence of Yb,Yb′Y_{b},Y_{b^{\prime}} gives 𝔼{ρυ(Yb,Yb′)∣Q,x}=p(Q)\mathbb{E}\{\rho_{\upsilon}(Y_{b},Y_{b^{\prime}})\mid Q,x\}=p(Q). There are exactly B⁡(B−1)B(B-1) such ordered pairs. Therefore the score in Equation 4.6 satisfies

𝔼⁡(S^∣Q,x)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\widehat{S}\mid Q,x) =BB​a​(Q,x)−B⁡(B−1)2​B​(B−1)​p​(Q)\displaystyle=\frac{B}{B}a(Q,x)-\frac{B(B-1)}{2B(B-1)}p(Q)
=a⁡(Q,x)−12​p​(Q)=Sυ​(Q,x).\displaystyle=a(Q,x)-\tfrac{1}{2}p(Q)=S_{\upsilon}(Q,x). (E.32)

This calculation uses linearity of expectation, not independence among the overlapping pair terms ρυ​(Yb,Yb′)\rho_{\upsilon}(Y_{b},Y_{b^{\prime}}). Moreover,

0≤1B​∑bρυ​(Yb,x)≤Ae,0≤12​B​(B−1)​∑b≠b′ρυ​(Yb,Yb′)≤Ae2.0\leq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\rho_{\upsilon}(Y_{b},x)\leq A_{\rm e},\qquad 0\leq\frac{1}{2B(B-1)}\sum_{b\neq b^{\prime}}\rho_{\upsilon}(Y_{b},Y_{b^{\prime}})\leq\frac{A_{\rm e}}{2}.

Subtracting these two nonnegative terms gives −Ae/2≤S^≤Ae-A_{\rm e}/2\leq\widehat{S}\leq A_{\rm e}, completing Equation E.29.

Step 2: bound the effect of one simulated endpoint. Let fx​(y1,…,yB)f_{x}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{B}) be the expression in Equation 4.6, with Xi=xX_{i}=x and Ym,i,b=ybY_{m,i,b}=y_{b}. Consider two input vectors y,y~∈𝒦eBy,\widetilde{y}\in\mathcal{K}_{\rm e}^{B} that agree except at coordinate bb. In the first average, only ρυ​(yb,x)\rho_{\upsilon}(y_{b},x) can change, and its change is at most AeA_{\rm e}. In the pairwise sum, only the 2​(B−1)2(B-1) ordered pairs involving coordinate bb can change; each change is at most AeA_{\rm e}. Thus

|fx​(y)−fx​(y~)|≤AeB+2​(B−1)​Ae2​B​(B−1)=2​AeB=:cb.|f_{x}(y)-f_{x}(\widetilde{y})|\leq\frac{A_{\rm e}}{B}+\frac{2(B-1)A_{\rm e}}{2B(B-1)}=\frac{2A_{\rm e}}{B}=:c_{b}. (E.33)

Step 3: prove the bounded-variable exponential inequality. Let VV be a centered real random variable taking values in an interval [a,a+c][a,a+c] of length c≥0c\geq 0. Define ψ⁡(t)=log⁡𝔼​et​V\psi(t)=\log\mathbb{E}e^{tV} for t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. Boundedness of VV justifies differentiation under the expectation. Under the exponentially tilted probability measure d​ℙt=et​V−ψ⁡(t)​d​ℙ\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{t}=e^{tV-\psi(t)}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}, these derivatives are

ψ′​(t)=𝔼t​V,ψ′′​(t)=Vart⁡(V),\psi^{\prime}(t)=\mathbb{E}_{t}V,\qquad\psi^{\prime\prime}(t)=\operatorname{Var}_{t}(V),

where 𝔼t\mathbb{E}_{t} and Vart\operatorname{Var}_{t} are expectation and variance under ℙt\mathbb{P}_{t}. The tilted law still assigns probability one to [a,a+c][a,a+c]. Since variance is the minimum squared distance to a constant,

0≤ψ′′​(t)≤𝔼t​{V−(a+c/2)}2≤c2/4.0\leq\psi^{\prime\prime}(t)\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}\{V-(a+c/2)\}^{2}\leq c^{2}/4.

The identities ψ⁡(0)=0\psi(0)=0 and ψ′​(0)=𝔼​V=0\psi^{\prime}(0)=\mathbb{E}V=0, followed by the integral form of Taylor’s formula, give, for every real tt,

ψ⁡(t)=t2​∫01(1−s)​ψ′′​(s​t)​𝑑s≤t2​c24​∫01(1−s)​𝑑s=t2​c28.\psi(t)=t^{2}\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)\psi^{\prime\prime}(st)\,\mathrm{d}s\leq\frac{t^{2}c^{2}}{4}\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)\,\mathrm{d}s=\frac{t^{2}c^{2}}{8}.

Consequently

𝔼​et​V≤exp⁡(t2​c2/8),t∈ℝ.\mathbb{E}e^{tV}\leq\exp(t^{2}c^{2}/8),\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}. (E.34)

The integral formula also covers t<0t<0, so no one-sided restriction on tt is being imposed. Applying the same argument under a conditional probability law proves the conditional version of Equation E.34 whenever the conditional mean is zero and the conditional range has length at most cc.

Step 4: derive the bounded-differences exponential inequality. Let Ξ1,…,ΞB\Xi_{1},\ldots,\Xi_{B} be independent random variables, and let f=f⁡(Ξ1,…,ΞB)f=f(\Xi_{1},\ldots,\Xi_{B}) be a bounded measurable function. ℱb=σ(Ξ1,…,Ξb),Mb=𝔼(f∣ℱb),Db=Mb−Mb−1,b=1,…,B,\mathcal{F}_{b}=\sigma(\Xi_{1},\ldots,\Xi_{b}),\qquad M_{b}=\mathbb{E}(f\mid\mathcal{F}_{b}),\qquad D_{b}=M_{b}-M_{b-1},\quad b=1,\ldots,B,

with ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} trivial and M0=𝔼​fM_{0}=\mathbb{E}f. Then ∑b=1BDb=f−𝔼​f\sum_{b=1}^{B}D_{b}=f-\mathbb{E}f and 𝔼⁡(Db∣ℱb−1)=0\mathbb{E}(D_{b}\mid\mathcal{F}_{b-1})=0.

For a dictionary of laws QmQ_{m}, the corresponding terms p⁡(Qm)/(2​B)p(Q_{m})/(2B) need not agree and cannot be treated as a common offset. ∎

Appendix F Details of the numerical studies

F.1 Neural models, training, and validation

All procedures use a two-dimensional encoder with an affine skip and two hidden ReLU layers of width 64. Encoder outputs are projected onto the Euclidean ball of radius four. Velocity and score heads have two hidden ReLU layers of width 64 and receive the response state, encoded context, and time. Head outputs are clipped to [−16,16][-16,16] coordinatewise, and state inputs to the neural residual are clipped to [−10,10][-10,10]. Layer weights and biases are projected to norm caps 12 and 5. The diffusion score is the neural residual minus the current state. Transfer procedures use a source-trained encoder and a fresh target head. TFM-Freeze and Tian–Shen keep the encoder fixed; adaptation updates it jointly with the target head. The Tian–Shen comparator implements the frozen-embedding transfer mechanism of Tian and Shen (2026) with this common architecture.

Positive-penalty adaptation uses an orthogonally aligned functional anchor,

Asrot​(h)=minQ∈O⁡(2)⁡1256​∑i=1256‖h⁡(za,i)−Q​h^s​(za,i)‖2,A_{s}^{\rm rot}(h)=\min_{Q\in O(2)}\frac{1}{256}\sum_{i=1}^{256}\|h(z_{a,i})-Q\widehat{h}_{s}(z_{a,i})\|^{2}, (F.1)

where the anchor contexts are drawn from the source sample. The orthogonal Procrustes solution is updated during training. This specifies the functional anchor used in the numerical implementation of Section 2.4. Positive penalties are selected from {0.01,0.1,1}\{0.01,0.1,1\}; the separately tuned unpenalized family fixes λ=0\lambda=0. The encoder/head learning-rate ratio is r=0.1r=0.1 for both adaptive families in all reported experiments.

FM uses G∼Nd​(0,Id)G\sim N_{d}(0,I_{d}) and T∼Unif⁡(0,1)T\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1), with interpolation (1−T)​G+T​X(1-T)G+TX and regression response X−GX-G. Diffusion uses the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck interpolation e−t​X+1−e−2​t​Ge^{-t}X+\sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}G on [0.01,4][0.01,4] and uniform-time denoising score matching, evaluated with log-uniform time sampling and the corresponding importance weights. Adam uses minibatches of size 128, head learning rates {10−3,3×10−4}\{10^{-3},3\times 10^{-4}\}, encoder weight decay 10−410^{-4}, and gradient-norm clipping at ten. Source encoder/head learning-rate ratios are 0.30.3 and 11; source and target checkpoints are {500,1500,3000,6000}\{500,1500,3000,6000\} and {250,750,1500,3000}\{250,750,1500,3000\} updates. Source encoders use regularized canonical correlation analysis (CCA) initialization. Target-only fits compare CCA initialization with encoder/head ratio 0.10.1 and random initialization with ratio 11.

Source observations are divided into fitting and tuning subsets in proportions 90/10, with at most 256 held-out rows used for source tuning. The target fitting, tuning, and validation counts are (614,205,205)(614,205,205) in the simulations, (153,51,52)(153,51,52) for Materials, and (1228,410,410)(1228,410,410) for Diamonds. Hyperparameters and checkpoints minimize the ensemble energy score on the tuning subset, using 48 generated responses and 128 field evaluations per response.

For each TFM procedure, the additional validation step compares its tuned candidate with tuned target-only FM. If DiD_{i} is the transfer score minus the target-only score on validation observation ii, transfer is retained when

D¯+Φ−1​(0.95)​sDng<0,\overline{D}+\Phi^{-1}(0.95)\frac{s_{D}}{\sqrt{n_{g}}}<0, (F.2)

where sDs_{D} is the sample standard deviation and ngn_{g} is the validation sample size. Otherwise target-only FM is retained. Each comparison uses 96 generated responses and 256 field evaluations per response, with paired random numbers. The three comparisons define separate reported procedures. Once tuning and validation choices are fixed, the selected specifications are fitted using all observations supplied to the repetition, with update counts multiplied by the full-to-fitting sample-size ratio and rounded upward. A validated procedure uses exactly its selected transfer or target-only fit and generated samples. Test observations are excluded from these fitting and selection steps.

F.2 Construction of the real-data samples

For Materials, the original data contain 21,263 materials and 81 predictors. Element counts are normalized to composition proportions and rounded to twelve decimal places. One recorded response per composition is retained using response-independent random priorities. The domain definitions in Section 6 leave 7155 source and 1347 target compositions. The latter comprise 1011 compositions eligible for training and the fixed test set of 336 compositions. Each repetition samples 6000 source and 256 target training compositions.

For Diamonds, we remove twenty records with nonpositive physical dimensions from the original 53,940 observations. Retaining one record per exact non-cut predictor vector by response-independent random priorities leaves 53,476 groups. Before applying the cut-grade domain definitions, half the groups are randomly assigned to a source-only cohort. Premium and Very Good cuts in that cohort form the source; Ideal cuts in the remaining cohort form the target. This construction yields 12,714 source and 10,585 target groups. The target groups are divided into 9561 eligible for training and 1024 reserved for testing. Each repetition samples 12000 source and 2048 target training groups. The nineteen predictors contain six numerical variables and reference-coded color and clarity indicators, with reference levels D and I1. Reported scores are on the log-response scales defined in the main text. The same 40 training seeds are used for both applications, and methods share the samples and fixed test set within an application.

F.3 Evaluation and uncertainty

For ρ⁡(x,x′)=‖x−x′‖/d\rho(x,x^{\prime})=\|x-x^{\prime}\|/\sqrt{d} and an ensemble X^1,…,X^M\widehat{X}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{X}_{M} generated at a context zz, the unbiased energy-score estimate at an observed response xx is

S^​(z,x)=1M​∑a=1Mρ⁡(X^a,x)−1M⁡(M−1)​∑a<bρ⁡(X^a,X^b).\widehat{S}(z,x)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{a=1}^{M}\rho(\widehat{X}_{a},x)-\frac{1}{M(M-1)}\sum_{a<b}\rho(\widehat{X}_{a},\widehat{X}_{b}). (F.3)

For d=1d=1, this is the ensemble CRPS estimator. In the simulations, an independent ensemble X1,…,XMX_{1},\ldots,X_{M} from the true conditional distribution also permits estimation of the unrooted energy discrepancy,

ℰ^​(z)=2M2​∑a,bρ⁡(X^a,Xb)−2M⁡(M−1)​∑a<b{ρ⁡(X^a,X^b)+ρ⁡(Xa,Xb)}.\widehat{\mathcal{E}}(z)=\frac{2}{M^{2}}\sum_{a,b}\rho(\widehat{X}_{a},X_{b})-\frac{2}{M(M-1)}\sum_{a<b}\{\rho(\widehat{X}_{a},\widehat{X}_{b})+\rho(X_{a},X_{b})\}. (F.4)

This unbiased estimate can be slightly negative. For q=1,2q=1,2, empirical Wasserstein distance is

W^q​(z)={minπ∈𝔖M⁡1M​∑a=1Mρ​(X^a,Xπ⁡(a))q}1/q.\widehat{W}_{q}(z)=\left\{\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{M}}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{a=1}^{M}\rho(\widehat{X}_{a},X_{\pi(a)})^{q}\right\}^{1/q}. (F.5)

Scalar ensembles are sorted; multivariate ensembles use separate equal-weight assignment problems for each cost. These are joint empirical distances and retain finite-ensemble error. All criteria are averaged over test contexts and then over training repetitions.

Final evaluation uses M=256M=256 generated responses and 512 field evaluations per response. FM uses 256 explicit-midpoint ODE steps; diffusion uses 512 Euler–Maruyama steps on a geometric reverse-time grid from four to 0.01, with Gaussian initialization and no terminal denoising. Evaluation streams are shared across methods and independent of training and selection streams. In the simulations, BB and CC are obtained once for each pp by seeded QR factorization. Source samples are nested across source sizes within a repetition; target observations and target-only fits are reused across those sizes. The 100 training repetitions within each setting are the units for Monte Carlo standard errors and Student-tt intervals.

For the real data, uncertainty is summarized by pointwise 95% paired Student-tt intervals across the 40 training repetitions. For each method contrast, let Δb\Delta_{b} be the difference in mean test CRPS within repetition bb. The interval is Δ¯±t39,0.975​sΔ/40\overline{\Delta}\pm t_{39,0.975}s_{\Delta}/\sqrt{40}, where sΔs_{\Delta} is the sample standard deviation of the 40 paired differences and t39,0.975t_{39,0.975} is the 97.5th percentile of the Student-tt distribution with 39 degrees of freedom. This describes variation across training repetitions conditional on the observed data pools and fixed target test set. We report Materials and Diamonds at r=0.1r=0.1.

A harmful repetition has a larger mean test criterion than its matched target-only fit, with tolerance 10−1210^{-12}. The criterion is energy discrepancy for simulations and CRPS for applications. The comparator is target-only FM for all TFM procedures and target-only diffusion for Tian–Shen. Exact fallback ties are excluded. Zero harmful repetitions describes performance in the reported experiment.

F.4 Supporting comparisons

At θ=0.5\theta=0.5 and ns=8000n_{s}=8000, the paired difference in mean energy discrepancy between unpenalized adaptation and TFM-Freeze is −0.0833-0.0833 for d=1d=1, with pointwise 95% interval [−0.0892,−0.0774][-0.0892,-0.0774]. For d=5d=5, the corresponding difference for TFM-Adapt is −0.0470-0.0470, with interval [−0.0507,−0.0434][-0.0507,-0.0434]. Both adaptive procedures improve on each of the five nonadaptive comparators in these dimensions after Holm adjustment over the 60 one-sided paired energy contrasts comparing four adaptive procedures (positive or zero penalty, with or without validation) with five nonadaptive controls in all three dimensions. Each adjusted pp-value for these d=1,5d=1,5 comparisons is below 10−410^{-4}.

Table 2 summarizes the effect of validation at ns=8000n_{s}=8000. At smaller source sizes in the unrelated regime, both adaptive procedures with validation also have zero harmful repetitions, except for one out of 100 when (p,d,ns)=(50,1,1000)(p,d,n_{s})=(50,1,1000). Validation can reject useful transfer: for related scalar responses at ns=8000n_{s}=8000, it retains the positive and zero-penalty fits in 49 and 51 repetitions, respectively. These decisions explain the separation between the adaptive curves with and without validation in the upper-left panels of the figures.

Table 3 gives the Diamonds comparisons that support the accuracy gains in the main text. Both penalties yield improvements over every nonadaptive comparator, whereas the difference between the two adaptive fits is small: −0.00007-0.00007, with pointwise 95% paired interval [−0.00024,0.00010][-0.00024,0.00010].
